what: Robert FitzRoy started a telegraph-based gale warning service for shipping in Britain.
fit: Storm warnings were issued ahead of time from measurements of weather collected by telegraph and charted.

sources.title: Weather forecasting
sources.quote: His warning service for shipping was initiated in February 1861, with the use of telegraph communications.

note: FitzRoy's 1861 telegraph-based gale warnings and Times forecasts were the first public forecasts from synoptic measurements. Rejected earlier: Le Verrier's 1854-55 storm-warning proposal (a retrospective analysis and network, not a forecast service), Richardson's 1922 hand-computed numerical forecast (failed), ENIAC numerical forecast 1950 (first computed forecast by calculation; later). Accuracy 'days in advance with precision' was modest in 1861, so confidence is medium-low.
searched: Wikipedia Weather forecasting, Numerical weather prediction.

what: Charcot's team at the Salpetriere in Paris had a motor-driven "vibrating chair" built to treat patients with Parkinson's disease, in constant use there by 1894.
fit: A chair that moves itself mechanically to act on the sitter, matching the massage-chair alias but not fitting itself to the user.

sources.title: Vibratory medicine
sources.quote: Dr. Jdgu caused to be constructed a "vibrating chair," which is in constant use at the Saltpetrikre

note: Dated the massage-chair alternative, a chair that moves itself by a motor; it does not reshape to fit the user, so the fit is loose and confidence low. Charcot's vibrating chair at the Salpetriere (c.1892, built by Gilles de la Tourette's circle for Parkinson's patients) is the earliest powered chair found; electric massage chairs were also in use by 1904 and Glenn Noble's "Electric Roller Chair" appeared in 1919-20 (Electrical Experimenter). Chairs that automatically adjust to the sitter (sleep-number beds with automatic firmness, scanning massage chairs, memory foam which reshapes passively from 1991) were considered and are later; no earlier genuine self-fitting furniture found.
searched: archive.org full-text search Charcot vibrating chair 1892-1905; Wikipedia Massage chair

what: Harvey Cushing used William Bovie's radio-frequency electrosurgical generator at Peter Bent Brigham Hospital, Boston, to remove a mass from a patient's head.
fit: A high-frequency electric knife that cuts tissue while coagulating it, so bleeding is controlled.

sources.title: Electrosurgery
sources.quote: The first use of an electrosurgical generator in an operating room occurred on October 1, 1926 at Peter Bent Brigham Hospital

sources.title: William T. Bovie
sources.quote: It was known, for example, that electric current above certain frequencies could cut tissue without inducing muscular contraction.

note: Earlier electrocautery and high-frequency work (d'Arsonval, Howard Kelly and others) is mentioned by Wikipedia but not dated; hot-wire cautery is not cutting by radio-frequency current. Laser and ultrasonic scalpels are later alternatives not dated. JAMA 1930 and NEJM 1929 describe Bovie units in use but are later than two years. No mass adoption date sourced (hyfrecator for office use 1940).
searched: Wikipedia Electrosurgery, William T. Bovie; archive.org search 'Bovie' Cushing 1926-1930.

what: Frigidaire marketed a split-system room cooler small enough for homes.

what: The first five Chain Home radar stations, covering the approaches to London, were installed on the south-east coast of Britain by 1937, forming the first early-warning radar network.

sources.quote: Chain Home was the first early warning radar network in the world and the first military radar system to reach operational status.

Daventry radar test (Feb 1935) and single-station detection (June 1935) were not networks.

note: Atmospheric theatres show an artificial sky with stars and clouds in an entertainment hall; the Majestic 1923 is Eberson's own claim as first, and the page does not describe its sky in detail (the stars-and-clouds quote is from the 1929 Akron theatre). Smell, music and mood generation (Sensorama 1962) are not covered. Considered and rejected: the Zeiss planetarium dome (Deutsches Museum, 1923; educational, not for entertainment or comfort), nineteenth-century panoramas and Kaiserpanoramas (painted scenes, not generated sky). The 1923 date comes from the architect's own claim.
searched: Wikipedia Atmospheric_theater; web search not run for panorama predecessors.

what: Willem Kolff implanted an artificial heart in a dog at the Cleveland Clinic; the dog lived 90 minutes.
fit: A mechanical heart implanted in a living animal that sustained circulation.

sources.title: Artificial heart
sources.quote: On 12 December 1957, Willem Johan Kolff, the world's most prolific inventor of artificial organs, implanted an artificial heart into a dog at Cleveland Clinic

note: Earlier external pump bypassing a dog's heart for an hour (Sewell and Glenn, Yale, 1949) was extracorporeal, not an implanted heart.
searched: Wikipedia Artificial heart, Ventricular assist device.

what: Domingo Liotta and E. Stanley Crawford implanted the first left ventricular assist device in a patient at Baylor, Houston.
fit: An implanted mechanical pump supporting a failing natural heart in a patient.

sources.title: Ventricular assist device
sources.quote: The first LVAD was implanted in 1963 by Liotta and E. Stanley Crawford

note: I used the definition's 'support' alternative. The first total artificial heart in a human was Liotta and Cooley on 4 April 1969 in Houston (a 64-hour bridge to transplant); the first successful LVAD support was 1966. No mass adoption: totals remain small.
searched: Wikipedia Artificial heart, Ventricular assist device.

what: John Abel, Leonard Rowntree and Benjamin Turner built the first artificial kidney (vividiffusion) and cleansed the blood of animals outside the body.
fit: A device passing blood outside the body through a dialysis membrane to remove wastes.

sources.title: Hemodialysis
sources.quote: The artificial kidney was first developed by Abel, Rountree, and Turner in 1913

note: Graham's dialysis principle (1854) was not a machine for blood.
searched: Wikipedia Hemodialysis.

what: Willem Kolff built a working dialyzer in 1943 in the Netherlands and treated uremic patients; his first survivor recovered in 1945.
fit: A machine filtering a patient's blood outside the body to substitute for failed kidneys.

sources.title: Hemodialysis
sources.quote: Willem Kolff was the first to construct a working dialyzer in 1943

sources.title: Kolff artificial kidney results
sources.quote: the artificial kidney may well have a life-saving action

note: Georg Haas performed the first human dialysis on 28 February 1924 in Giessen, but those experimental treatments did not help patients, so I treated Kolff's patient treatment (1943) as first practical use; the date would move to 1924 if Haas's attempts count.
searched: Wikipedia Hemodialysis; archive.org search for Kolff artificial kidney 1943-1946.

what: A 1972 US law made Medicare cover dialysis for end-stage renal disease at any age, making treatment routine for patients.
fit: Dialysis routinely used by ordinary patients with kidney failure.

sources.title: Kidney dialysis
sources.quote: Since a 1972 law, government insurance (Medicare) covers the cost of dialysis and transplants

note: Scribner's shunt (1960) and Alwall's earlier treatment of many patients (1946-60) preceded wide use; 1972 is a policy date, not a measured adoption date.
searched: Wikipedia Hemodialysis, Kidney dialysis.

what: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds built SNARC (40 vacuum-tube neurons, Navy-funded) at Princeton; it learned to solve a maze.

sources.title: SNARC
sources.quote: They tested the machine on a copy of Shannon's maze, and found that it could learn to solve the maze.

sources.title: Marvin Minsky
sources.quote: In 1951, Minsky built SNARC, which is often considered the first artificial neural network.

note: Earlier than the first pass (Rosenblatt's perceptron 1957-58). McCulloch and Pitts (1943) was a non-learning mathematical model, not a built machine; Farley and Clark (1954) simulated a Hebbian network on a computer, later than SNARC. Exact month of SNARC working not found (funded summer 1951).

what: Bell Labs applied convolutional neural networks trained by backpropagation (LeNet) to handwritten digit recognition for zip codes, later reading cheques in ATMs.

sources.title: LeNet
sources.quote: In 1989, Yann LeCun et al. at Bell Labs first applied the backpropagation algorithm to practical applications

note: Widrow and Hoff's ADALINE (1960) and MADALINE (largest built 1963) adaptive filters are described by Wikipedia as 'likely the first artificial neural network applied to a real-world problem' (phone-line echo removal), which would be earlier, but I found no dated first deployment. The CIA studied the Mark I Perceptron 1960-64 only as an evaluation.

what: Jacques Loeb at Woods Hole made unfertilized sea urchin eggs develop into larvae (plutei) with salt solutions, with no sperm.
fit: Eggs were induced chemically to develop into living larvae without any male parent, which is artificial parthenogenesis.

sources.title: Jacques Loeb (1859-1924)
sources.quote: Loeb earned his reputation as a biologist-engineer in 1899 when he published experimental results showing artificial parthenogenesis in sea urchins

note: Rejected Tichomiroff 1886 (sulfuric acid on silkworm eggs, a species that also develops parthenogenetically unaided; only embryos seen). Later firsts: Loeb frog larvae and adults around 1910; Kaguya bimaternal mouse 2004 (Kono). No human case.

what: Sputnik 1 launched into Earth orbit by the Soviet Union and circled the Earth for three months.
fit: A man-made object placed in Earth orbit that stayed up and circled it.

sources.title: The progress of science: Internationalise space now
sources.quote: On Friday, October 4, 1957, the first artificial satellite was launched.

sources.title: Sputnik 1
sources.quote: was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on 4 October 1957

note: Earlier suborbital or orbit-failed attempts (V-2 and Vanguard TV-3 are later or non-orbital) were rejected. Relay/communication use: first relay satellite SCORE (1958-12) and Echo 1 (1960) came later; Sputnik's radio beacon was its practical (ionosphere/tracking) use, so both kinds share the date.
searched: archive.org periodicals 1957; Wikipedia Sputnik 1.

sources.quote: 1952 - Bell Labs researchers, Stephen Balashek, R. Biddulph, and K. H. Davis, built Audrey for single-speaker digit recognition.

what: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, reports seeing napkins woven of asbestos flax thrown into fire and coming out clean, and funeral cloths for kings made of it.
fit: Cloth woven of asbestos fibre shown to be fireproof.

sources.publisher: The History Blog (quoting Pliny, Natural History XIX.4, tr. Bostock and Riley)
sources.title: Ancient sources on asbestos
sources.quote: napkins that were made of it thrown into a blazing fire, in the room where the guests were at table

note: Earlier candidates: Chinese 'fire-laundered cloth' claims for the Zhou dynasty (Wikipedia: not substantiated; certain accounts date to the Wei dynasty, 4th-6th century AD); Persian asbestos napkins (7th century); asbestos-ceramic pottery in Finland ~4,500 years ago (pottery, not cloth); Pausanias (2nd century AD) lamp wick. Pliny (AD 77) is the earliest firsthand account found of woven asbestos cloth, which he says he saw tested in fire and used for royal funeral cloths. Pliny's book date AD 77 is taken from general knowledge, not the page quoted. Asbestos paper was not dated.
searched: Wikipedia Asbestos; The History Blog quoting Pliny; Perseus/Thayer Pliny page returned 404.

what: Livy reports that in 331 BC many leading Romans died of a malady taken for pestilence, which a serving-woman revealed to be secret poisoning by matrons, who were then tried.
fit: Secret poisoning that mimicked a natural epidemic, matching killing by induced illness resembling natural death.

sources.publisher: Perseus Digital Library (Livy, tr. B. O. Foster)
sources.title: Livy, History of Rome 8.18
sources.quote: those whose deaths made the year notorious for pestilence were in reality destroyed by poison

note: Livy himself doubts the story and writes about 300 years later, so the event is uncertain. Later well-documented cases: Claudius (AD 54), the 1957 Rebet cyanide-gas pistol and 1978 Markov ricin pellet (concealed devices). Earlier undocumented poisonings (Egypt, India) were not found.
searched: WebSearch for Livy 8.18; Perseus Livy 8.18; Wikipedia Locusta, Poison.

what: Pioneer 10 traversed the asteroid belt (1972-07-15 to 1973-02-15) with a meteoroid detector and found no large particles; the belt is sparse and safe.
fit: A spacecraft crossing the belt measured how crowded it is and whether it is hazardous.

sources.title: Pioneer 10
sources.quote: No fragments larger than a millimeter were detected, indicating that such objects were much rarer than expected.

sources.title: Pioneer 11 Jupiter encounter
sources.quote: PIONEER 10 ENTERS ASTEROID BELT

note: Ground-based estimates of belt mass (19th-20th century) were inferred, not measured in situ, so rejected. Contemporary source only dates the crossing; the finding rests on the reference.
searched: Wikipedia Pioneer 10 and Asteroid belt; archive.org NTRS Pioneer reports.

what: NASA's DART spacecraft hit asteroid Dimorphos, shortening its orbit around Didymos by 32 minutes (confirmed 2022-10-11).
fit: An asteroid was redirected into a new orbit, though by kinetic impact rather than gravity or thrusters, so the fit is on function.

sources.title: NASA confirms DART probe impact changed asteroid's orbit
sources.quote: shaving 32 minutes off the time needed to complete one orbit around a parent asteroid known as Didymos

sources.title: Double Asteroid Redirection Test
sources.quote: they confirmed that the impact shortened Dimorphos's orbital period by 32 minutes

note: Mechanism differs from the definition's gravity or thrusters. No capture into Earth orbit and no gravity-tractor or thruster redirection has been done. Dimorphos is a moonlet, whose orbit around Didymos changed, not the Didymos system's solar orbit.
searched: Wikipedia DART, web search.

what: A synoptical table of orbital elements of all known small planets was published (Lespiault, reprinted by the Smithsonian), compiled from Medler's Astronomy and Astronomische Nachrichten.
fit: A systematic tabulation of asteroid orbital elements used for reference and charting.

sources.title: Annual Report of the Board of Regents 1861 (Lespiault, Remarks on the small planets)
sources.quote: We terminate this paper with the table of the elements of the small planets, prepared from the last edition of the Astronomy of M. Medler

note: Earliest not established: ephemerides of the first asteroids already ran in the Berliner Astronomisches Jahrbuch from the 1800s, and Medler's earlier edition is the table's source. The Minor Planet Center (Cincinnati, 1947) is later. This 1861 table is the earliest I could fetch, so the date is an upper bound.
searched: archive.org full text 1840-1900 for tables of elements of small planets; Wikipedia Minor Planet Center, Berliner Astronomisches Jahrbuch.

what: Gaia Data Release 1 gave positions, parallaxes and proper motions for about 2 million stars (plus positions of 1.1 billion).
fit: An instrument survey measured positions, parallaxes and proper motions for millions of stars.

sources.title: Gaia Data Release 1. Summary of the astrometric, photometric, and survey properties
sources.quote: contains the positions, parallaxes, and mean proper motions for about 2 million of the brightest stars

sources.title: Gaia (spacecraft)
sources.quote: The first data release, Gaia DR1, based on 14 months of observation was on 14 September 2016.

note: Earlier surveys only partly fit: Astrographic Catalogue/Carte du Ciel (first plate 1891-08, positions of millions, no parallaxes), Bonner Durchmusterung (1859-62, ~324,000 stars, positions), Hipparcos (1997, 118,000 stars with parallaxes), Tycho-2 (2000, 2.5 million, positions and proper motions only). Gaia DR1 is the first with all three quantities for millions. If the definition is read loosely, the AC would date to about 1900.
searched: Wikipedia Astrographic Catalogue, Gaia, Tycho-2; Semantic Scholar for Gaia DR1.

what: NASA chose the Mercury Seven (announced 1959-04-09) under a height limit of 5 ft 11 in and age under 40, set by the capsule's size.
fit: Astronauts were selected by body size (and an age cap) to suit a small capsule.

sources.publisher: US Senate Committee on Aeronautical and Space Sciences
sources.title: Project Mercury: Man-in-Space Program of NASA
sources.quote: under age 40; and 5 feet 11 inches in height or less.

sources.title: Mercury Seven
sources.quote: The height limit was a function of the design of the Mercury spacecraft, which could not accommodate someone taller.

note: Soviet cosmonaut group (1960) also had height and weight limits but is later. Selecting for small stature to save cost, or for the elderly, matches only in part: this is a maximum-size rule. John Glenn's 1998 flight at 77 (selected for aging research) is later. Same event serves both kinds.
searched: archive.org NTRS Senate Mercury report 1959; Wikipedia Mercury Seven.

sources.quote: It was first used by astronaut Ed White during the first American "spacewalk" (extra-vehicular activity, EVA), on Gemini 4, June 3, 1965.

fit: A handheld thruster carried a spacewalker between objects for a mission task.

sources.title: Hand-held maneuvering unit

searched: Wikipedia HHMU, MMU, Gemini 10.

what: Air Force Man High balloon project selected its crew by psychiatric interviews on motives and emotional stability, a claustrophobia test and a week of stress tests, as a model for choosing astronauts.

what: Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson discovered the ozone layer from the missing ultraviolet in the Sun's spectrum at the ground.
fit: A layer of the upper atmosphere was shown to absorb solar ultraviolet radiation.

sources.title: Ozone layer
sources.quote: The ozone layer was discovered in 1913 by French physicists Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson.

note: Dated the existence of the radiation-shielding layer: Fabry and Buisson's 1913 solar spectrum showed UV below about 310 nm absorbed by ozone. Earlier: Hartley 1881 proposed ozone absorbs solar UV (page text not found, not used). The 'can be broken' part was shown by the Antarctic ozone hole (Farman et al., Nature, 1985), later. Discovery concept: only first_demonstration.
searched: Wikipedia Ozone layer.

what: Fog-collection fences built in South Africa as a water source for an air force base, averaging 11 liters a day over 14 months.
fit: Condensation of airborne moisture on collecting surfaces produced usable water without any other source.

sources.title: Fog collection
sources.quote: One of the first recorded projects of fog collection was in 1969 in South Africa as a water source for an air force base.

note: Fog fences condense water from air on surfaces and delivered water for a base; this is the earliest dated, documented working project found. Source says 'one of the first', so earlier cases may exist.
searched: Wikipedia Atmospheric water generator, Air well (condenser), Fog collection, Fuel cell, Gemini 5; archive.org search on Gemini fuel-cell drinking water (lending-library books, no text).

what: William Potts of the Detroit police installed automatic four-way, three-color traffic lights in 15 towers across Detroit.
fit: Lights ran automatically at intersections without a police officer giving signals, matching lights regulating traffic without human signals.

sources.title: Traffic light
sources.quote: In 1921, he installed automatic four-way, three-color traffic lights in 15 towers across Detroit.

note: Earlier: 1868 London gas semaphore lamp (manually operated), 1912 Lester Wire Salt Lake City and 1914 Cleveland electric lights (police operated), 1920 Potts Detroit (manual). Later computer control: Toronto 1954 (Casciato and Kates), Denver 1952. note: Source is a 2024 retrospective, so reference only. It was a prototype that never went into production. what: Heinrich Lamm, a medical student in Munich, transmitted an image through a bundle of flexible glass fibres bent around curves, aiming to look inside the body.
fit: Light carried along a curved path lets the viewer see around an obstacle, here for inspecting hidden body cavities.

sources.title: Heinrich Lamm
sources.quote: When Lamm was a medical student in 1930, he developed the first flexible fiber-optic bundle capable of transmitting images around curves.

sources.title: Fiber-optic communication
sources.quote: Heinrich Lamm showed that one could transmit images through a bundle of unclad optical fibers and used it for internal medical examinations

note: Dated alternative: image carried by light along a bent fibre bundle so a viewer sees around corners (Lamm, 1930). Rejected: Roth and Reuss, Vienna, late 1800s (light guided through bent glass rods to illuminate body cavities, illumination only); Colladon and Babinet 1840s and Tyndall 1854 (light guided in a water jet, no viewing); gravitational lensing and Airy beams (2007, curved beams that do not let one view hidden objects); non-line-of-sight imaging (2012) uses scattered light, not a curved beam. Practical use: Lamm used it on internal exams per Wikipedia but with poor image quality; the first practical fibre endoscope (Hirschowitz, 1957) is later and I did not find a usable source for first patient use, so no separate practical date. Mass adoption not claimed.
searched: Wikipedia Fiber_optic, Heinrich_Lamm, Endoscope; archive.org search 1957-59 for fiberscope (no hits).

sources.quote: upon transmitting a few shocks through the thorax, he perceived a small pulsation; in a few minutes the child began to breathe

Prevost and Batelli 1899 (dog defibrillation, Geneva) and Beck 1947 (first human internal defibrillation) are later and narrower. what: Louis Bertrand Castel's second, improved ocular harpsichord, which opened a colored glass pane for each key, was demonstrated to a small audience in December 1754.
fit: A keyboard instrument that plays colors of light in correspondence with music.

sources.quote: A second, improved model of the harpsichord was demonstrated for a small audience in December 1754.

note: Castel proposed the instrument in 1725; Wikipedia says Telemann went to see it in 1739, but whether the first model was ever completed is disputed, so the documented 1754 demonstration is used. Later candidates: Bainbridge Bishop color organ patent 1877, Rimington Colour-Organ 1895, Telharmonium and Theremin (1897-1920), Hammond organ 1935.
searched: Wikipedia Color organ, Louis Bertrand Castel.

what: Alexander Wallace Rimington demonstrated his Colour-Organ at St James's Hall, London, in 1895 and gave further concerts there and in Manchester, accompanying music by Chopin and Wagner.
fit: A keyboard instrument projected mixed colored light onto a screen in public performances alongside music.

sources.title: Alexander Wallace Rimington

what: The Hammond organ, an electric organ first manufactured in 1935, was bought by over 1,750 churches in its first three years, and an estimated two million were produced.
fit: Electronic organs became common instruments for churches and homes.

sources.title: Hammond organ
sources.quote: Over 1,750 churches purchased a Hammond organ in the first three years of production

note: Light-music devices never became common; this milestone is for electronic organs only. Synthesizers became common in the late 1960s-70s (not sourced).
searched: Wikipedia Hammond organ.

what: Thomas Sutton photographed a tartan ribbon through red, green and blue filters for James Clerk Maxwell's 1861 lecture; the three images projected together gave a full-color picture.
fit: Natural colors were recorded photographically without hand-tinting, by the three-color method.

sources.title: Color photography
sources.quote: with the first color photograph produced by Thomas Sutton for a Maxwell lecture in 1861

note: Earlier direct-color attempts: Edmond Becquerel (1848-51) and Niepce de Saint-Victor recorded colors on silver plates but the colors could not be fixed and faded in light, and Levi Hill's Hillotype (about 1850) was unreliable (Wikipedia). Seebeck's 1810 colors on silver chloride were spectrum effects. These are rejected as non-lasting, but a stricter reading could date the first demonstration to 1848-1850.
searched: Wikipedia Color photography; archive.org search for Maxwell/Sutton 1861 (no usable hit).

what: The Lumiere Autochrome plate, a single-plate color process using dyed starch grains, reached the market in 1907 and amateurs and professionals took it up.

sources.quote: has been steadily on the increase among local photographers

searched: Wikipedia Color photography; archive.org Photo-Era 1908.

what: Halley's Comet reached perihelion on 13 March 1759, delayed 618 days by Jupiter and Saturn, as Clairaut, Lalande and Lepaute had computed (within a month).
fit: Planetary perturbation of a comet's orbit was predicted by calculation and confirmed by observation, which establishes the orbit half of the claim.

sources.quote: the attraction of Jupiter and Saturn having caused a delay of 618 days

note: I dated the orbit-perturbation half. Considered Halley's 1705 prediction (no perturbation test yet) and Lexell's comet (1770). what: At the outbreak of the Indian Rebellion (Meerut/Delhi, May 1857) the mutineers cut the telegraph wires, leaving British stations cut off from news.

searched: WebSearch on earliest telegraph cutting; Wikipedia Electric telegraph, Indian Rebellion of 1857; archive.org full-text search for wires cut 1857 (found The Examiner 1857-07-04).

sources.title: Antitoxin
sources.quote: On 4 December 1890, Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō published their first paper on blood-serum therapy.

note: Dated serum from immune animals (antitoxin), the alternative the definition allows ('immune animals'); serum from human survivors (convalescent plasma) came later in use for other diseases. Behring and Kitasato's first paper is 4 December 1890 (Deutsche medizinische Wochenschrift); Tizzoni and Cattani (Bologna) published tetanus antitoxin work at about the same time and independently. Earlier immunity ideas (Jenner, Pasteur vaccines) are active vaccination, not transfer of serum. Sources conflict on the 1891 human use: one says Behring saved a girl in 1891, another says the 1891 human trials were unsuccessful and successful treatment began in 1894.

what: Josiah Latimer Clark installed a 220-yard pneumatic tube in London between the Stock Exchange and the Electric Telegraph Company, passing capsules of messages by air pressure; it was used in daily service to carry stock prices.
fit: A pipe moved carriers of messages (orders and price information) across part of a city by air pressure with no vehicle or person carrying them, but the cargo was paper messages, not goods or food.

sources.title: Pneumatic tube
sources.quote: he installed a 220-yard (200 m) pneumatic system between the London Stock Exchange in Threadneedle Street, London, and the offices of the Electric Telegraph Company

note: Considered: London Pneumatic Despatch Company (1863-1874), which carried mail, parcels and light freight but used rail trucks driven through the tube, so vehicles; 1865 Berlin and 1866 Paris pneumatic post networks (letters, not freight); 1865 Pithole oil pipeline in Pennsylvania (a long-distance pipe for goods, but not urban and not the earliest oil pipe I could source). Messages are a loose stand-in for goods, so confidence is low.

sources.title: Plastic surgery
sources.quote: In 1891, American otorhinolaryngologist John Roe presented an example of his work: a young woman on whom he reduced a dorsal nasal hump

note: Rejected as reconstructive, not aesthetic: Sushruta's nasal reconstruction (by 800 BC) and Tagliacozzi's 1597 nasal reconstruction after mutilation; John Orlando Roe's 1887 endonasal rhinoplasty, which treated saddle-nose deformity. Roe's 1891 hump reduction on a young woman is the earliest case in the sources that is explicitly for cosmetic indication. Wikipedia also cites cosmetic operations from the Renaissance and earlier (labiaplasty, Heister's blepharoplasty) without dates or cases I could verify; Jacques Joseph's reduction rhinoplasty (1898) and Holländer's facelift (1901) are later.

what: Harold Spencer Jones showed that fluctuations in the apparent longitudes of the Sun, Moon and planets came from variations in the Earth's rotation rate, establishing that the length of the day changes.
fit: A measurement from astronomical records established that the Earth's spin speed varies, i.e. changes in the length of the day.

sources.publisher: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
sources.title: The Rotation of the Earth, and the Secular Accelerations of the Sun, Moon and Planets
sources.quote: The Rotation of the Earth, and the Secular Accelerations of the Sun, Moon and Planets

sources.title: Spencer Jones, Harold
sources.quote: he proved—qualitatively, but quite definitely—that the fluctuations in the observed longitudes of these celestial bodies

note: Earlier suspicions rejected as not established: Halley's 1695 and later 18th-century noting of the Moon's secular acceleration, and tidal-friction theory (Kant 1754, Delaunay and Ferrel 1860s). Stephenson and Morrison's ancient-eclipse analysis (1984) later quantified the long-term slowing. The Earth has not stopped or become tidally locked to the Sun.
searched: WebSearch; Crossref DOI 10.1093/mnras/99.7.541; Wikipedia Earth's rotation, Tidal acceleration (no history found), encyclopedia.com

what: Catalina Sky Survey discovered 2006 RH120 on 14 September 2006, a 2-7 m natural object that was temporarily captured in orbit around Earth until mid-2007.

sources.title: 2006 RH120
sources.quote: 2006 RH120 was discovered on 14 September 2006 by Eric Christensen with the 27-inch (690 mm) Schmidt camera of the Catalina Sky Survey in Arizona.

sources.title: Dynamics of Asteroid 2006 RH120: Pre-Capture and Escape Phases
sources.quote: Asteroid 2006 RH120 was the first natural object captured by the Earth to be observed called a Minimoon.

note: Dated the temporary-satellite alternative: no permanent second moon exists. Rejected: 1991 VG (discovered 1991-11, temporarily captured but did not complete a full orbit and its capture was noted later); Kordylewski dust clouds (1961, dust, disputed); 19th-century claims (Petit 1846, Pickering's 1900s) never confirmed; Cruithne (1986) is a co-orbital, not a satellite; 2020 CD3 later. A permanent second moon has not been found.
searched: Web search on minimoons; read Wikipedia Temporary satellite, 2006 RH120, 1991 VG, NASA NTRS record.

what: On Apollo 8, Borman, Lovell and Anders became the first humans to see the whole Earth at once, a colored globe, then the crescent Earth and the first Earthrise at the Moon.

sources.title: Apollo 8
sources.quote: this marked the first time humans had viewed the whole Earth at once.

note: Earlier cameras (not observers): V-2 photos 1946, Explorer 6 TV scan 1959-08-14, Lunar Orbiter 1 took the first Earth pictures from the Moon in 1966-08, ATS-3 color full-disk 1967-11. Earlier humans in orbit (Gagarin 1961, Glenn 1962 saw city lights of Perth) saw only part of the Earth, so not the globe. Google Earth-style routine viewing by the public is a loose analogue, so no mass_adoption.

what: Newton's Principia proved that a hollow shell exerts no net force on anything inside it and that force inside a uniform sphere falls in proportion to distance from the center, reaching zero at the center.
fit: This is the principle that gravity weakens inside the Earth as one descends, vanishing at the center, derived mathematically from the inverse-square law.

sources.title: Shell theorem
sources.quote: no net gravitational force is exerted by the shell on any object inside, regardless of the object's location within the shell

sources.title: Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica
sources.quote: first published in 1687

note: A derivation, not a measurement. For the real Earth, density rises with depth so gravity first increases to about the core-mantle boundary and falls to zero only below it (seismic Earth models from the 1930s-40s, PREM 1981); Airy's 1854 Harton mine pendulum experiment found gravity larger at depth. Newton's theorem is the earliest establishment of the principle itself.
searched: Wikipedia Shell theorem, Gravity of Earth, PREM

what: Edward L. Withey (Instrument Research Co., Brighton, Mass.) described an experimental cathode-ray tube, the Peritron, whose phosphor screen oscillates in depth inside a vacuum globe so that moving spots appear at true positions in three dimensions (proposed for air-traffic control).
fit: A volumetric display, not a hologram: a swept-screen CRT that draws changing points in a real 3-D volume seen in a viewing globe, so the picture is a true volumetric one rather than a stereo pair; the definition's 'holographic' wording is only its label.

note: Replaces second pass 1962 (static optical holograms), which the definition and test cases exclude (a static hologram is not a display of changing images). Candidates rejected: Parker/Wallis 'Three-dimensional cathode-ray tube displays' (IEE 1948) and MacKay's 'projective' displays (1949) only rotate a 3-D plot into a 2-D view, no volumetric picture; the 1962 optical holograms and Cross's 1972 multiplex hologram are static or fixed-sequence recordings; Traub's varifocal-mirror display (Applied Optics, 1967-06) and ITT's rotating-screen air-traffic display (Aviation Week 1960-10-31, 'gives 3-D effect from any viewing angle without need for stereoscopic illusion', working small-scale model) are later but clearly fit. Earlier volumetric proposals exist (1912 postulate) but no working device was found before Withey's.

what: NASA's MOXIE instrument on the Perseverance rover produced 5.37 g of oxygen from Martian carbon dioxide in Jezero Crater.
fit: A crew-oriented resource (oxygen) was extracted on another world from local material, but the feedstock was atmospheric CO2 rather than the rock, ice or soil the definition names.

MOXIE is the earliest actual extraction of a resource on another world, but from atmosphere, so only partly matches rock/ice/soil; no rock, ice or soil extraction on a body has been done as far as found. note: Earlier candidates rejected: a 1940 rumor of German 'sleeping gas' in Belgium (Science News Letter 1940-05-25, unverified, methyl bromide guess); 1960s US BZ (a delirium-producing anticholinergic, not a knock-out gas, never used operationally); plant-poison incapacitation (Hannibal 184 B.C., 1881 Tuareg dates) not a gas; WWI tear gas (irritant, not knock-out); individual chloroform use not delivered by gas device at scale. what: NCD-RisC (Imperial College) pooled 1,472 population studies of 18.6 million people and measured how average adult height rose across 200 countries for people born 1896-1996 (South Korean women +20.2 cm, Iranian men +16.5 cm).
fit: Measurement established that average adult height rose substantially, by diet and health, over a century in most countries.

sources.title: A century of trends in adult human height
sources.quote: The largest gain in adult height over the past century has occurred in South Korean women and Iranian men

note: This is a global compilation, not the earliest observation. National conscript series (e.g. Norway from 1878, Switzerland from 1878-79, Netherlands) already showed rising height in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and Villermé (1829) linked height to living conditions, but I did not retrieve a page giving an exact earlier date for the first documented rise, so the date is a late bound. Rejected: pre-1850 'no change since Neolithic' data in Wikipedia Human height (no rise yet).
searched: WebSearch secular trend/Villermé/Quetelet/Bowditch; archive.org search 'increase in stature' conscripts 1880-1950 (US Army 1921 anthropology volume, Bowles 1932; lending item unreadable); Wikipedia Human height; Crossref eLife 2016.

what: Julius Gudernatsch fed thyroid gland to frog tadpoles, which started metamorphosing into frogs within days, weeks before untreated controls.
fit: A substance (thyroid tissue) fed to an organism speeds it through its life cycle (metamorphosis) in days to weeks; this dates the life-cycle alternative, not evolutionary change.

sources.title: Heredity and sex
sources.quote: The tadpoles might begin their metamorphosis in a few days after the first application of the thyroid, and weeks before the control animals did so

note: Gudernatsch's paper is Arch. Entw.-Mech. 1912. Later: directed evolution of Qβ RNA in a test tube (Spiegelman 1967) is evolution in hours but not an organism; plant growth regulators (gibberellin, ethylene) shift timing but are less dramatic. No earlier hormone speed-up found.
searched: archive.org search Gudernatsch 1912-1914; read Morgan 'Heredity and Sex' (1913).

what: John Cockcroft and Ernest Walton at the Cavendish Laboratory bombarded lithium with accelerated protons and observed it split into two alpha particles, releasing about 16 MeV per disintegration.
fit: Swift protons trigger the splitting of a stable atom (lithium-7) and the nucleus releases energy, as the definition requires; the energy released exceeds the energy of the incoming particle.

sources.title: Disintegration of Lithium by Swift Protons (Cockcroft and Walton)
sources.quote: The evolution of energy on this view is about sixteen million electron volts per disintegration

note: Rutherford's 1919 nitrogen-to-oxygen transmutation by alpha particles was rejected: it is endothermic, so it did not release energy. Joliot-Curie artificial radioactivity (1934) and Hahn-Strassmann uranium fission (December 1938, Frisch and Meitner 'Disintegration of uranium by neutrons', February 1939) are later. The Cockcroft-Walton letter gives the energy only as a 'view' pending confirmation, and I dated it to the April 1932 submission and publication.
searched: Wikipedia reading plus archive.org full-text search for 'Disintegration of Lithium by Swift Protons' (1932); read the Nature 1932-04-30 issue.

what: The United States dropped a uranium fission bomb ('Little Boy') on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945, the first use of triggered atomic splitting to release energy on demand outside a test.
fit: A neutron chain reaction splits uranium atoms and releases their energy at a chosen moment, which is the definition's on-demand energy release.

sources.title: The Bombay Chronicle, 8 August 1945
sources.quote: Atom bomb, which has more than 2.003 times the blast power

sources.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
sources.quote: On 6 August, a Little Boy was dropped on Hiroshima.

note: Earlier controlled releases were experiments: Chicago Pile-1 (1942-12-02), the X-10 Graphite Reactor (1943) and the Trinity test (1945-07-16). Hanford B reactor (September 1944) produced plutonium but I did not source it. The first reactor electricity (Obninsk, 1954-06) is later. The quote is the OCR text of the newspaper's report of the Truman announcement. I do not claim a mass_adoption date: nuclear power never became something ordinary people use directly.
searched: Wikipedia plus archive.org full-text search for 'atomic bomb' Hiroshima in August 1945 newspapers.

what: Carl von Linde in Germany liquefied air by compressing it and letting it expand through a regenerative cooling cycle, and obtained oxygen and nitrogen from the liquid air.
fit: Air is liquefied by machinery and separated into its component gases, which is the definition's mechanism, though at working-demonstration rather than industrial scale.

sources.title: Carl von Linde
sources.quote: in 1895 he succeeded in liquefying air by first compressing it and then letting it expand rapidly, thereby cooling it.

note: Earlier liquefaction of air or oxygen in small quantities by Cailletet and Pictet (1877) and Wroblewski and Olszewski (1883) did not produce a working method for separating the gases. Hampson built a similar air liquefier in 1895 as well, so the order within the year is unclear. Brin's barium oxide oxygen process (1886) separated oxygen from air on a commercial scale but chemically, not by liquefaction or similar machinery, so I did not date it.
searched: Wikipedia Air separation, Carl von Linde, Liquefaction of gases; archive.org searches for Linde liquid air oxygen 1895-1904 (contemporary text found only for Dewar and Linde's liquefier, no usable quote).

what: Linde's liquid-air process was first used in an industrial application in 1902, supplying oxygen and nitrogen separated from air.
fit: Air is liquefied and fractionated by machinery on an industrial scale to supply oxygen and nitrogen commercially, matching the definition.

sources.title: Air separation
sources.quote: the process remained purely academic for seven years before it was used in industrial applications for the first time (1902)

note: Georges Claude's air-liquefaction oxygen plant in France was also started in 1902, so it is a co-candidate that I could not separate from Linde. I found no contemporary source quickly. Brin's chemical process (1886) is rejected as above. Mass adoption not claimed: I found no source for the year it became routine for ordinary people.
searched: Wikipedia Air separation and Carl von Linde; archive.org searches for 1902-1904 trade periodicals (no usable quote).

what: Castaways from the wrecked ship Grafton on the Auckland Islands (1864-65) built a forge and made charcoal to work metal, burnt shells for lime mortar and made soap from what they could salvage or gather.

sources.title: Grafton wreck and Epigwaitt
sources.quote: Published accounts detail how the party built their own forge to work metal and made charcoal to fire it.

note: This is a documented example, not a verified earliest: similar shipwreck improvisation (e.g. the 1565 French wreck forge in Florida, Sea Venture at Bermuda 1609, Invercauld and General Grant 1864-66) is older or contemporary, and none produced glass or smelted ore. Fit is partial (salvaged iron reworked, not smelting from ore); no source found for an earliest event, so treat as a representative case.

what: A. C. Perdeck displaced more than 11,000 migrating starlings from the Netherlands to Switzerland: adults corrected toward the original wintering area, while inexperienced juveniles kept flying the inherited compass direction (southwest).
fit: Young birds that had never migrated flew an inborn compass direction without map or guide, showing an inherited direction sense.

sources.publisher: Wildlife Review (US Fish and Wildlife Service abstract of Perdeck, Ardea 6, 1958)
sources.title: Wildlife Review No. 97
sources.quote: After displacement, the adults aimed nw. to the original wintering area, and the juveniles aimed sw. to France and the Iberian Peninsula.

sources.title: Discovery 1953-05
sources.quote: Evidence has accumulated that such birds possess an innate tendency to fly in a certain compass direction.

note: Earlier work: Gustav Kramer's cage experiments on starlings (1949-1952, sun compass and migratory restlessness direction) and Rüppell's 1930s-40s displacement of crows; Discovery (May 1953) already says evidence of an innate compass tendency had accumulated, so the first demonstration is probably around 1949-1952. I did not retrieve a page giving the exact Kramer date, so 1958 is a late bound. Homing pigeons' return was known since antiquity but not shown to be inborn.
searched: archive.org search Perdeck, Kramer starlings 1950-1962; Wikipedia Magnetoreception/Animal navigation (Wiltschko 1972 robins magnetic compass, later).

what: Mariner 10's first Mercury flyby (29 March 1974) completed the measurement of surface conditions for the four bodies, after Mariner 4 (Mars, 1965), Venera 7 (Venus surface, 1970) and the Luna and Apollo landings (Moon).
fit: Spacecraft measurements of atmosphere, surface temperature and pressure gave the facts about all four bodies, the last being Mercury in 1974.

sources.title: Mariner 10
sources.quote: The first Mercury encounter took place at 20:47 UTC on 29 March 1974

sources.title: Mariner 10
sources.quote: The mission objectives were to measure Mercury's environment, atmosphere, surface, and body characteristics

sources.title: Venera 7
sources.quote: It was found that the temperature at the surface of Venus was 475 ± 20 °C

note: The concept bundles four bodies; I dated the point when all four had been measured by spacecraft. fit: The machine changed its response from the experience of paired stimuli (a neutral switch came to light the bulb after training, with extinction, forgetting and spontaneous recovery) instead of being wired for that response.

note: Moves the second pass's 1951 (SNARC) back to 1950 (Theseus, built 1950; shown at the 1951 Macy cybernetics conference and in Bell Labs press in 1952). Other candidates: Ashby's Homeostat 1948 (adapts to disturbances by random search for stability, closer to self-regulation, rejected), Grey Walter's tortoises 1948 (no learning; his conditioned-reflex version is 1951), Samuel's checkers program (1952 running, 1959 paper), Rosenblatt's perceptron 1957-58, Thomas Ross's 1930s maze-solving machine discussed in Psychological Review 1935 (could not read a description in the available text, so not used). Hull and Baernstein's working conditioning machine was published in 1929, and Hull built a related one with Krueger (named in Scientific American, April 1933, which also describes Thomas Ross's 1933 maze-learning machine with relay memory cells; Ross is later than Hull-Baernstein and was not used). The Science note lists the phenomena the machine reproduced (acquisition, extinction, reinforcement, spontaneous recovery, and so on). Not found: any earlier working learning machine; Stephens 1929 (cited in Psychological Bulletin 1931) was not read and is no earlier than mid-1929.

The magnetic mountain and a ship-dragging pull were never confirmed (Gilbert rejected a magnetic island).

note: A pre-modern natural phenomenon, so the date is a lower bound from reference sources (at least 2,500 years), not a dated first event. Other ancient candidates, none shown earlier: Baku fires/Ateshgah, Baba Gurgur near Kirkuk, Homer's Chimaera (Iliad) which may refer to this site. No first_demonstration or mass_adoption: it is a natural event, not a built device; the practical-use kind is used for the landmark/beacon role.

what: John Blankenbaker designed the Kenbak-1, a TTL-logic 8-bit computer intended for individuals and schools.

sources.title: Kenbak-1
sources.quote: Designed in 1970 by John Blankenbaker

note: Date is the design year; no exact date of a working prototype was found. Rejected as earlier: Wikidata's 1957 (IBM 610 Auto-Point was single-operator but a costly office machine), LINC (1962, a laboratory minicomputer), Olivetti Programma 101 (1965, programmable calculator) and Datapoint 2200 (June 1970, a terminal). The Computer History Museum, per Wikipedia, calls the Kenbak-1 the first personal computer.

what: The Kenbak-1 went on sale in early 1971 at about $750 (fewer than 50 built).

sources.title: Kenbak-1
sources.quote: was first sold in early 1971

note: Earlier than the first pass (Altair 8800, Jan 1975). Micral N (early 1973) was the first microprocessor-based PC. Very few units sold, so use was marginal.

what: The Brantly B-2, a two-seat light helicopter designed for private buyers, first flew.
fit: A small two-seat helicopter designed to be owned and flown by individuals.

sources.title: Brantly B-2
sources.quote: decided to design a simpler and less complicated helicopter for the private buyer

sources.title: Brantly B-2
sources.quote: first flew on 21 February 1953

note: Bell 47 (certified for civilian use 1946-03-08; first civilian delivery to an air-transport firm) was not aimed at private owners. Robinson R22 (first sale 1979) is later. No source showed individual owners flying one as everyday transport, and none showed mass adoption, so no practical use or mass adoption.

what: Jerónimo de Ayanz y Beaumont's air-renovated diving suit let a man stay underwater in the Pisuerga river on 2 August 1602, for an hour, before King Philip III ordered him back.
fit: A worn suit with a renewed air supply let a person survive a hostile environment (underwater) for an hour, matching the suit-plus-personal-air function.

sources.title: Timeline of diving technology
sources.quote: 1602: Jerónimo de Ayanz y Beaumont built an air-renovated diving suit that allowed a man to remain underwater in the Pisuerga river on August 2.

note: The concept's examples (respirators, heat and radiation suits, mirror suits) point at air, heat or radiation hazards; I took the underwater suit as the earliest strict fit for a hostile environment, which is a judgment. Other, later candidates for respirators: Pliny's bladder dust masks (1st century, dust only, not survival), Humboldt's mine respirator 1799, Deane smoke helmet patent 1823, Tyndall fireman's respirator 1871, WWI gas hoods (British Smoke Hood June 1915). If only gas or smoke protection counts the date moves to 1799 or later. Single reference source.
searched: Wikipedia Timeline of diving technology, Respirator, Diving helmet, Gas mask, John Lethbridge.

what: John Lethbridge's airtight oak diving barrel, invented in 1715, was used to salvage valuables from wrecks including English men-of-war, East Indiamen and Spanish galleons.
fit: A person wearing a sealed protective apparatus with its own air worked in a hostile environment (underwater) for a real commercial purpose, salvage.

sources.title: Timeline of diving technology
sources.quote: successfully used it to salvage valuables from wrecks

sources.title: John Lethbridge
sources.quote: known for inventing the first underwater diving machine in 1715

note: Date is the invention year; his best-known recovery (Slot ter Hooge, Madeira) came later, about 1724. Earlier: de Beauve's 1715 hosed dress (no use record found), Fréminet's machine used over ten years before 1784 (later). Same underwater-suit judgment as the demonstration. No mass_adoption given: civilian gas masks (about 38 million issued in Britain by 1939) and later industrial respirators are issue items, not routine use, and I did not fetch a source.
searched: Wikipedia Timeline of diving technology, John Lethbridge, Diving helmet.

what: Levitt Luzern Custer built an electric wheelchair at the Dayton Soldiers' Home, Ohio, for wounded veterans.
fit: A self-propelled, electric chair steered by its rider for individual trips.

sources.title: Motorized wheelchair
sources.quote: An early motorized wheelchair was invented by Levitt Luzern Custer in 1919

note: Dated the electric chair alternative because the name says electric. Autoped gasoline stand-up scooter (1915) is not electric. Electric tricycle by R.A. Harding (1920s) later. George Klein's production electric chair (after WWII) and the Sears electric chair (1954) were not dated well enough to give a practical-use date. Segway (2001) is later.
searched: Wikipedia Motorized wheelchair, Mobility scooter, Autoped, Wheelchair, Segway.

what: Smith & Wesson began producing its Safety Hammerless (New Departure) revolver, whose back-strap lever had to be squeezed by a correct grip before it could fire.
fit: A grip safety blocks firing unless the gun is held correctly, one of the definition's 'only when held correctly' mechanisms.

sources.title: Smith & Wesson Safety Hammerless
sources.quote: the revolver incorporated an internal hammer and an external grip safety on its back-strap

sources.title: The Collector's Friend: Vol. I, February 1889
sources.quote: or double action, Safety Hammerless

note: Dated the 'only when held correctly' alternative (a grip safety), not an owner-coded or biometric gun. Considered: Iver Johnson 1897 trigger-lever safety (later), Savage 1907/Colt 1911 grip safeties (later), Armatix iP1 and other owner-keyed smart guns (2010s, far later and not mass-marketed), 1980s location-locked gun patents (patents only). I did not find an earlier grip safety than S&W's 1887 revolver, but did not exhaustively search pre-1887 patents. The 1889 advertisement shows the model on sale but does not itself mention the grip safety. Integral key locks and owner-coded guns never became routine, so no mass_adoption.
searched: WebSearch on earliest grip safety pistols; Wikipedia Grip safety, Smart gun, S&W Safety Hammerless; archive.org full-text search 'safety hammerless' 1887-1890.

what: Trastuzumab (Herceptin) approved by the FDA in September 1998 for breast cancer patients selected by a laboratory test of HER2 status.
fit: A drug given only to patients whose own tumor chemistry (HER2 overexpression) is shown positive by examination, i.e. therapy tailored to the individual patient's biochemistry; this is the stratified form, not drug synthesis for one person.

sources.title: Trastuzumab
sources.quote: Trastuzumab was approved for medical use in the United States in September 1998

sources.title: Trastuzumab
sources.quote: Doctors use laboratory tests to discover whether HER2 is overexpressed.

note: Considered: Garrod's chemical individuality (1902) and the 1950s G6PD/isoniazid acetylator pharmacogenetics (discoveries of variation, not tailored treatment with a documented first dose-tailoring event); therapeutic drug monitoring and insulin dosing by glucose tests (loose, population-level adjustments); n-of-1 synthesized drugs such as milasen (2018, later). Possibly earlier individualized dosing exists but was not established in sources I could fetch.
searched: WebSearch pharmacogenetics history; Wikipedia Pharmacogenomics, Trastuzumab.

what: Adolf Butenandt characterized bombykol, the female silkworm moth sex attractant, the first pheromone chemically identified.
fit: A defined chemical scent shown to attract males of another individual of the species, i.e. a chemical signal controlling behavior.

sources.title: Bombykol
sources.quote: Discovered by Adolf Butenandt in 1959, it was the first pheromone to be characterized chemically.

note: Considered: 1950s insect attractant studies and Karlson and Luscher's coining of 'pheromone' (1959), same year; ant trail and queen-substance work (1950s) is not chemically defined. Repelling, enraging or disabling via scent has no separate earlier clear event.
searched: Wikipedia Bombykol, Pheromone, Pheromone trap; WebSearch gypsy moth disparlure.

what: Bliss and Lomo reported long-lasting potentiation of synaptic transmission in the rabbit dentate gyrus after perforant path stimulation (long-term potentiation).
fit: A persistent, stimulation-induced change in the strength of neural connections demonstrates a physical, electrical-cellular trace that could store memory.

sources.title: Long-lasting potentiation of synaptic transmission in the dentate area of the anaesthetized rabbit
sources.quote: In fifteen out of eighteen rabbits the population response recorded from granule cells in the dentate area to single perforant path volleys was potentiated

note: Considered: Hebb's 1949 cell-assembly proposal (theory only); Kandel and colleagues' Aplysia habituation synaptic change (1970), which may be earlier and equally fitting; Penfield's electrical stimulation recall (1930s-50s, no trace shown); Lashley's engram search (failed). Wikipedia also puts Lomo's first observation at 1966, unpublished. Date picked is the first full publication I could fetch.
searched: Wikipedia Long-term potentiation; PMC. Aplysia 1970 not verified.

what: Auguste Piccard and Max Cosyns reached 16,201 m (53,150 ft) in a pressurized-gondola hydrogen balloon.
fit: A crewed aircraft (a balloon) flew above ten miles (52,800 ft).

sources.title: Flight altitude record
sources.quote: 1932: 16.201 km (53,150 ft) -Auguste Piccard and Max Cosyns in a hydrogen balloon.

sources.title: Hong Kong Telegraph 1932-08-19
sources.quote: beat his own balloon ascent

note: I dated the balloon, the earliest crewed flight over ten miles. Piccard's 1931 flight (51,770 ft) fell just short. For heavier-than-air craft: Iven Kincheloe flew the Bell X-2 to 126,200 ft on 1956-09-07, the first piloted climb over 100,000 ft. U-2 operational flights (1956) and Concorde (1976) not sourced. Date of 18 August is from the Hong Kong Telegraph's 18 August dateline and the Wikipedia entry gives only 1932.
searched: Wikipedia Flight altitude record, X-2, MiG-25; archive.org search for Piccard 1932.

what: Sperry's Curtiss-Sperry Flying Bomb, launched from a moving Marmon car at Farmingdale NY, flew unmanned for the preset 1,000 yards under gyroscopic autopilot.
fit: A pilotless, self-propelled flying vehicle designed as a bomb flew itself over a set distance by autopilot, the guided unmanned flight the definition describes (it did not carry a warhead).

sources.title: Hewitt-Sperry Automatic Airplane
sources.quote: For the first time in history, an unmanned, heavier-than-air vehicle had flown in controlled flight.

note: Earlier: Hewitt-Sperry Automatic Airplane flights of Sept-Nov 1917 had a human pilot for take-off (rejected); Kettering Bug first flight 1918-10-02 failed, later flights in Oct 1918 were later than March 1918; 1849 Austrian balloon bombs were unpowered and unguided. The 1918-03-06 flight could not be repeated for a time, so confidence is low.
searched: Wikipedia Hewitt-Sperry Automatic Airplane, Kettering Bug, Cruise missile.

what: Germany launched V-1 flying bombs against London one week after D-Day.
fit: The V-1 was an unmanned, pulsejet-propelled, gyroscope-guided bomb that flew to its target without a pilot.

sources.title: V-1 flying bomb
sources.quote: The Wehrmacht first launched the V-1s against London on 13 June 1944

sources.title: Invasion Journal
sources.quote: Flying bombs came over all day and all night

note: Earlier candidates: Hewitt-Sperry/Kettering test aircraft 1917-18 (never used operationally), Fritz X/Hs 293 guided bombs 1943 (unpowered, dropped by aircraft so not self-propelled). The 1944 V-1 attack is the first operational use of a powered pilotless bomb.
searched: Wikipedia V-1 flying bomb, Cruise missile; archive.org full-text search 'flying bomb' London 1944. No mass_adoption: not a consumer technology.

what: Wired Radio, Inc. (North American Co.) first tested music over electric light wires into Cleveland residences from 15 March 1935.
fit: Music supplied continuously from a central studio to rooms through wires and loudspeakers.

sources.title: Heinl radio business letter (July-Dec 1935)
sources.quote: Following a three months' test of wired radio in Cleveland

sources.title: Broadcasting 1936-02-01
sources.quote: recently tested in Cleveland residences

note: Rejected: Telharmonium (1906, New York), which sent live synthesized music over telephone lines to hotels and restaurants, because I could not confirm continuous piping to concealed speakers and treat it as a looser analogue; Theatrophone (opera by telephone, not continuous background music). Squier's earlier wire tests (c.1922) are undated in sources I fetched.
searched: archive.org full text 1934-1937 (Variety, Broadcasting, Telephony, Heinl); Wikipedia Muzak, Telharmonium.

what: Muzak began its paid wired music service to New York hotels, restaurants and clubs on 16 March 1936; over 300 subscribers by November.
fit: Continuous recorded music piped from a central studio to many public rooms.

sources.title: Telephony 1936-11-28
sources.quote: The company pro- viding this program service started it last March 16.

note: Cleveland 1935 was a residential test; earlier commercial service by Wired Radio in Cleveland in 1934 is claimed but I did not find a dated source.

what: Alvarez, Alvarez, Asaro and Michel reported iridium spikes in Italy, Denmark and New Zealand at the Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary and proposed that an asteroid impact darkened the Earth and caused the extinctions; the Chicxulub crater was identified in 1991.
fit: A cosmic impact event that changed Earth's climate (global darkness and extinctions) was first established by this extraterrestrial iridium measurement, matching 'asteroid or cosmic event alters Earth's climate'.

sources.title: Extraterrestrial Cause for the Cretaceous-Tertiary Extinction
sources.quote: Deep-sea limestones exposed in Italy, Denmark, and New Zealand show iridium increases of about 30, 160, and 20 times

sources.title: Chicxulub crater
sources.quote: Hildebrand, Penfield, Boynton, Camargo, and others published their paper identifying the crater in 1991.

note: Dated the asteroid-impact-alters-climate alternative. The 1980 paper is the first measurement; many scientists accepted it only after the 1991 crater identification, so a later date (1991) is arguable. Not matched: a passing planet altering gravity, orbit or axial tilt, which has not happened. Earlier impacts such as Tunguska (1908) and Meteor Crater (proved 1903-1906) did not change global climate.
searched: Crossref and Wikipedia for the Alvarez paper and Chicxulub.

what: NASA's DART spacecraft struck the asteroid Dimorphos, shortening its orbit around Didymos by about 32 minutes (confirmed 2022-10-11).
fit: A spacecraft deliberately changed an asteroid's orbit by kinetic impact, the deflection technique of the definition (on a harmless target).

sources.title: Aruba Today (October 12, 2022)
sources.quote: Nelson said the impact shortened the as- teroid’s orbit by about 32 minutes.

sources.title: Double Asteroid Redirection Test
sources.quote: The collision shortened Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos by 32 minutes, greatly in excess of the pre-defined success threshold of 73 seconds.

note: Earlier candidates: Deep Impact (2005) hit a comet but changed its orbit immeasurably and was not meant as deflection; Cold War-era nuclear-deflection studies were proposals. No first_practical_use: no real impactor threat has been deflected. Cometary/asteroid capture and destruction have not happened. No mass adoption.
searched: Wikipedia DART; archive.org 2022 newspapers; NASA site (404 on one URL).

what: China destroyed its own Fengyun-1C weather satellite with a ground-launched kinetic kill vehicle.
fit: A ground-launched interceptor struck and destroyed an orbiting spacecraft, the weapon-from-the-ground function the definition names.

sources.title: The Characteristics and Consequences of the Break-up of the Fengyun-1C Spacecraft
sources.quote: The intentional break-up of the Fengyun-lC spacecraft on 11 January 2007 via hypervelocity collision with a ballistic object

sources.title: 2007 Chinese anti-satellite missile test
sources.quote: was destroyed by a kinetic kill vehicle traveling with a speed of 8 km/s

note: Earlier candidates: Soviet Cosmos 252 co-orbital interceptor 1968-11 (launched from the ground but is an orbiting satellite weapon, not a ground battery); US Program 505 (Nike Zeus) and Program 437 (Thor) ASATs, operational 1962-64 but no actual destruction of a satellite; 1985 US ASM-135 (air-launched). If Cosmos 252 is accepted as a 'ground-launched' weapon the date would be 1968. No practical use: no spacecraft has been destroyed in a defensive role from the ground; the only test was against the owner's own satellite.
searched: Wikipedia Anti-satellite weapon, Program 437, 2007 Chinese ASAT test; archive.org NTRS search 'Fengyun'.

what: Babylonian Text M: a computed ephemeris of the last evening visibility of Mercury for the years 424-403 BC, system A3.
fit: A table of dated planetary positions and appearances computed by arithmetic procedure, the dated forecast of planetary positions the definition describes.

sources.publisher: Archive for History of Exact Sciences
sources.title: A study of Babylonian planetary theory III. The planet Mercury
sources.quote: ephemeris of the last evening visibility of Mercury which turned out to have been computed according to system A 3 for the years 424–403 BC

note: Whether Text M was computed ahead of the years it covers or later is not stated in the text I read, so the date is the period it covers. Earliest surviving ephemeris tablet (ACT 300, Mercury) covers 309-289 BC; Venus tablet of Ammisaduqa (about 1600 BC) lists observations, not forecasts; Kepler's 1630 ephemerides predicted the 1631 transit (see practical use).
searched: Wikipedia Ephemeris, Babylonian astronomy, Babylonian astronomical diaries; Springer paper; WebSearch for oldest ephemeris.

what: Gassendi observed the transit of Mercury that Kepler had forecast in his 1630 ephemerides.
fit: A forecast of a planetary transit, dated in advance, was used to organize an observation and was confirmed by it.

sources.title: Transit of Mercury
sources.quote: The first observation of a Mercury transit was observed on November 7, 1631 by Pierre Gassendi.

sources.title: Transit of Mercury
sources.quote: Johannes Kepler had predicted the occurrence of transits of Mercury and Venus in his ephemerides published in 1630.

note: Babylonian astronomers used ephemerides for astrology and records long before, but I found no sourced use event, so the first well-documented use of a forecast for observation is dated here. Mass adoption (yearly almanacs: Connaissance des Temps 1679, Nautical Almanac 1767) is plausible but left out as I did not source routine use by ordinary people.
searched: Same as above; Wikipedia Ephemeris, Nautical Almanac.

what: B. P. Sharpless found from observations that Phobos's orbit is changing (secular acceleration, orbital decay toward Mars).
fit: A moon was shown by measurement to be drifting to a new orbit over time, which fits 'moons drift'.

sources.title: Bevan Sharpless
sources.quote: best known for his 1944 discovery that the orbit of Phobos was decaying

note: Date is the 1944 discovery per Wikipedia; Sharpless's paper is cited as 1945 by a 1957 MNRAS article. Rejected the Moon's secular acceleration (Halley 1695, Dunthorne 1749): it was an apparent mean-motion change whose cause (tidal drift of the Moon outward, with Earth's rotation slowing) was understood later and measured by laser ranging only in the 1970s (Calame and Mulholland 1978). Hot-Jupiter migration and Solar System migration (1980s-90s) are model inferences, not direct observations. Planets swapping places or moving toward/away from the Sun were not observed; this milestone dates only the moon-drift alternative. No practical use or mass adoption.
searched: Wikipedia Tidal acceleration, Phobos, Planetary migration, Bevan Sharpless; Crossref; archive.org MNRAS 1957, Sky and Telescope 1951.

what: NASA adopted spacecraft sterilization and decontamination as national policy in December 1960 (first applied to the Ranger series).
fit: A binding rule to sterilize probes so they do not carry Earth germs to other worlds.

sources.title: Effect of Sterilization in Spacecraft Design
sources.quote: the National Aeronautics and Space Administration in December, 1960 authorized spacecraft sterilization and decontamination as National policy

sources.title: Planetary protection
sources.quote: which met for a year and recommended that interplanetary spacecraft be sterilized

note: Considered: 1956 IAF Congress raising the problem and the 1958 NAS resolution/CETEX recommendation (advice, not a rule); Apollo 11 lunar quarantine (1969) is a later implementation of the return side (Lunar Receiving Laboratory) and was not dated as the earliest. Ranger probes were the first required to be sterilized, with difficulties.
searched: WebSearch Ranger sterilization; NTRS; Wikipedia Planetary protection, Interplanetary contamination, Lunar Receiving Laboratory.

sources.quote: Lunokhod 1 rover, delivered to the Moon by the L-una 17 spacecraft in November 1970

what: Samuel Morey of New Hampshire patented and demonstrated (New York, Philadelphia; boat and wagon) an internal combustion vapor engine running on spirit of turpentine, with alcohol substitutable for water in the mixture; described in the Franklin Institute Journal in August 1826.
fit: An engine burned fuel made from plants (turpentine from pine resin, ethanol) to power a boat and a wagon in place of steam and mineral fuel.

sources.title: Boston Masonic Mirror 1826-11-25: Vol 2 Iss 48
sources.quote: we ex- amined a new vapor, or explosive engine, lately invented by Col. Samvet Morey

sources.title: Samuel Morey
sources.quote: Morey demonstrated his engine in New York and Philadelphia and there are eyewitness reports for both.

note: Earlier: de Rivaz's 1807 engine burned hydrogen (not plant fuel); Lenoir (1860) used coal gas; Otto's early engines (1860s) ran on alcohol-bearing mixes later. what: Sugarcane ethanol began to be used as motor fuel in Brazil in the late 1920s and early 1930s, as automobiles arrived.
fit: Cars ran on ethanol from sugarcane, blended with or in place of gasoline, in ordinary service.

sources.title: Ethanol fuel in Brazil
sources.quote: The first use of sugarcane ethanol as a fuel in Brazil dates back to the late 1920s and early 1930s

note: This is the earliest I could source, not necessarily the world's earliest; alcohol-fueled stationary and farm engines in Europe around 1900 and Diesel's 1900 peanut-oil engine likely came first, but I did not find a source that I could fetch. searched: Wikipedia Ethanol fuel in Brazil, Ethanol fuel in the United States, Alcohol fuel; archive.org search for German alcohol motors 1899-1902 (no useful hit).

what: In Brazil more than 4 million cars and light trucks ran on pure ethanol by the late 1980s, about a third of the country's vehicle fleet, after the Fiat 147 ethanol car launched in July 1979.
fit: Ordinary drivers routinely used cars fueled by plant-derived ethanol in place of gasoline.

sources.title: Ethanol fuel in Brazil
sources.quote: more than 4 million cars and light trucks running on pure ethanol by the late 1980s, representing one-third of the country's motor vehicle fleet

Chemical residue of a plant poison (buphandrine, epibuphanisine) was found on quartz arrowheads at Umhlatuzana, South Africa (Isaksson et al., Science Advances 2026). what: Willem Barentsz's crew wintered on Novaya Zemlya (about 76 N) in 1596-97; the sun sank to the horizon in early November and did not reappear until 24 January 1597, the first recorded European observation of the months-long polar night, with a long continuous daylight period known to follow.
fit: A dated first-hand record of the sun staying away for about eleven weeks at a polar latitude establishes the months-long polar night (and, by symmetry, the summer sun that circles without setting).

sources.publisher: Hakluyt Society (Gerrit de Veer, Three Voyages of William Barents, ed. Beke)
sources.title: The three voyages of William Barentz to the Arctic regions (1594, 1595, and 1596)
sources.quote: The most remarkable occurrence during their stay in Novaya Zemlya, was the unexpected reappearance of the sun on the 24th of January, 1597.

sources.title: Pytheas
sources.quote: He is also the first person on record to describe the midnight sun.

note: Earlier: Pytheas of Massalia (c. 325 BC) described the midnight sun at Thule, but his account survives only in paraphrase and reports short nights, not months of continuous day or night; the Greek theory of a frigid zone with six-month days was known but unobserved. Indigenous peoples certainly knew the polar night earlier but left no dated record. The January 1597 date is when de Veer's party saw the sun return; the 1876 introduction is a reference, but de Veer's own narrative (1598, Dutch) is the primary source and I did not fetch it. Concept is a fact about the world, so no practical-use or mass-adoption kinds.

what: Edison's Holborn Viaduct station in London began running on 12 January 1882, supplying electricity to street lamps and private customers over a distribution network.
fit: A central generating station feeding lines that supply lamps and customers, the first public electricity network, though it was a district network not yet a regional grid.

sources.title: Holborn Viaduct power station
sources.quote: The plant began running on 12 January 1882

note: Godalming's 1881 water-driven plant powered street arc lights and some private customers and is a rival first for combined public/private supply but was tiny and local. Regional transmission with transformers was shown at Lauffen-Frankfurt in 1891 (175 km, 15 kV) and a national synchronised grid in Britain in 1933; those fit 'regional' better but came after a working distribution network, so the earliest network event is dated. Pearl Street (New York, September 1882) came later.
searched: Wikipedia Holborn Viaduct power station, Godalming, Electric power transmission, National Grid (Great Britain).

fit: Bomb fallout contaminated inhabited islands so that residents had to be evacuated and Bikini remained uninhabitable for decades.

note: Hiroshima and Nagasaki (1945) were resettled and Trinity (1945) sat in empty desert, so not 'made uninhabitable'. Bikini was cleared in 1946 for tests, which was planned evacuation not fallout. what: After a B-52 crash at Palomares, Spain (Jan 1966), US and Spanish teams stripped plutonium-contaminated topsoil and plowed lightly contaminated fields to make them usable again.
fit: Radioactively contaminated ground was cleaned by removing and burying topsoil and plowing, so it could be farmed again.

sources.publisher: W. H. Langham, The Problem of Large-Area Plutonium Contamination
sources.title: The Problem of Large-Area Plutonium Contamination
sources.quote: areas with readings greater than 500 yug/m? were stripped of top soil and the contaminated soil, debris, and vegetation returned to the United States

sources.title: 1966 Palomares B-52 crash
sources.quote: A total of 2.2 hectares (5.4 acres) was decontaminated this way, producing 6,000 barrels.

note: Removal and burial is the physical method, not the burning, rays or accelerated decay of fiction, and some contamination remains. Operation Crossroads (1946) decontaminated ships, not ground; Bikini and Enewetak soil removal came later (1969, 1977-80). Chemical (WWI gas) and biological (Gruinard Island anthrax, 1986) ground decontamination were considered but I found no sourced earlier case. Langham's paper is dated 1968, a little over two years after the event, so reference.

what: Apollo 15's orbiting gamma-ray spectrometer (July-August 1971) detected natural radioactivity (potassium, thorium, uranium) of the Moon and mapped its strongest concentrations in Mare Imbrium and Oceanus Procellarum.
fit: Instruments measured radiation from large radioactive-element-rich regions of another world (the thorium and uranium bearing KREEP terrain), though these are enriched rock, not rich ore bodies.

note: Weak fit: no uranium or radium ore deposits whose radiation affects landers has been found anywhere; the Moon only has regions modestly enriched in U and Th. Earlier lunar gamma-ray measurements (Luna 10, 1966) found rock comparable to basalt, not a deposit. Kept as a low-confidence stand-in; the reviewer may drop it. Mars Odyssey and Lunar Prospector (1998) mapped Th later.

what: Apollo 15 heat flow experiment (Langseth, Columbia University), deployed at Hadley Rille in July 1971, measured heat flowing out of the Moon's interior; the preliminary report attributed it probably to radioactive heat generation in the interior.
fit: A moon's interior is shown to be warm from heat that leaks out, and the measurement is interpreted as radioactive decay heating, matching the radiogenic-heat mechanism (no subsurface ocean).

sources.quote: probably results from radioactive heat generation in

sources.title: Heat-Flow Experiment
sources.quote: The heat flow experiment installed on the lunar surface during the Apollo 15 flight is described

note: The interpretation was tentative ('probably'). Earlier candidates: meteorite-parent-body heating by 26Al (1976 discovery) is later; Galileo-era Ganymede/Europa oceans (1990s) are later and tidal rather than radiogenic. The Earth's Moon is the dated moon. The 1971 date is the deployment/first data year.
searched: WebSearch; NTRS and the Apollo 15 PSR text.

note: Case reported to the Royal Humane Society (founded 1774): a three-year-old pronounced dead after a fall from a window was given electric shocks through the chest and began to breathe. Historians dispute whether it was true cardiac revival or arousal from coma, and the account is retrospective, so confidence is low. Rejected as later or not revival of the dead: Beck's 1947 human defibrillation (a heart in fibrillation on the table), Gurvich 1939 and Negovsky 1930s animal resuscitation, Brukhonenko's 1920s dog experiments, Kouwenhoven CPR 1960. Wikipedia lists Prevost and Batelli 1899 defibrillation in dogs, which is later.

what: Frank Sprague's electric railway and motor company introduced regenerative braking, in which the drive motor returns power to the supply system.
fit: The motor acts as a generator while braking and returns the energy to the supply for reuse by other vehicles.

note: Single reference with no contemporary confirmation found (archive.org searches for 1885-1892 gave no hits). Krieger's Paris electric cars of the 1890s also had regenerative brakes (year not given); the Orwell truck came in WWI; the Milwaukee Road electrification described in 1917 returned about 60 percent of climbing power on descents.
