what: A 2003 American Horticultural Society draft hardiness map, from 1986-2002 data, placed many US areas about half a zone warmer than the USDA 1990 map; the official 2012 USDA map confirmed most of the US a half zone warmer in winter.
fit: Winters in temperate regions became lastingly milder so that plants of warmer zones can be grown farther north.

sources.title: Hardiness zone
sources.quote: The 2003 map placed many areas approximately a half-zone higher (warmer) than the USDA's 1990 map.

note: Only the 'milder' part came true, by about 2.8 C in winter minimums; no region became semitropical (no pineapples in England, no tree ferns on the Hudson). Callendar showed in 1938 that land temperature had risen over the previous 50 years, a global not regional finding. Very loose fit, kept at low confidence.
searched: Wikipedia Hardiness zone, USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, Callendar effect, Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation.

what: Antoni van Leeuwenhoek moistened dried gutter dust and saw living rotifers swim after drying; repeated with boiled water and dryings of months.
fit: Desiccated animals were restored to active life by adding water.

sources.title: Effects of Desiccation on the Rotifer
sources.quote: This was the first observation to be made on the phenomenon of desiccation with subsequent revival in animals

note: Leeuwenhoek (letter published 1702) believed the animals were not truly dried, but the revival observation stands. Dated animals (rotifers); no human revival exists. Later tardigrade work (Spallanzani 1776) is later. No practical use or mass adoption found.
searched: archive.org journal full text; Wikipedia Rotifer.

what: Walter Kaufmann measured the deflection of fast beta-ray electrons and found their charge-to-mass ratio fell as speed rose, showing mass increases with velocity.
fit: A body's effective mass was measured to rise with speed near light speed (electrons at a large fraction of c).

sources.title: Kaufmann-Bucherer-Neumann experiments
sources.quote: thus demonstrating that mass or momentum increases with velocity

note: Kaufmann's 1901 data initially favored Abraham's non-relativistic electron model; Bucherer (1908) first agreed with the relativistic formula and Neumann (1914/15) confirmed it. I dated the first measurement of velocity-dependent mass. If only the relativistic formula counts, the date is 1908. First practical use: particle accelerators (synchrocyclotron, 1946) compensate for it, but I did not source it.
searched: Wikipedia KBN article.

what: Ives and Stilwell measured the Doppler shift of hydrogen canal rays moving toward and away from the observer; the center of the lines shifted as predicted by time dilation.
fit: Moving atoms' clocks were shown to run slow by the Lorentz factor (a speed far below light speed, but the same effect).

sources.title: Ives-Stilwell experiment
sources.quote: The experiment was performed in 1938

note: Rossi and Hall (1941) used muons at about 0.99c, Hafele-Keating (1971) flew clocks on airliners; both later. Earlier tests like Michelson-Morley bear on length contraction only. No travelers have approached light speed, so no practical or mass milestone.
searched: Wikipedia Time dilation and Ives-Stilwell.

what: At McCook Field, Dayton, Ohio, Capt. R. E. Vaughn drove a small driverless three-wheeled car (about 8 ft long) through city traffic by radio from a car following behind.

searched: archive.org full text 1921 radio controlled automobile Dayton; Wikipedia Houdina Radio Control, Unmanned ground vehicle; NYT 1925-07-28.

searched: archive.org full text for 'fired by wireless' and 'exploded by wireless' 1895-1915; Wikipedia Ilya Starinov; web search on Soviet radio mines.

searched: web search for first radio-controlled detonation; Wikipedia Ilya Starinov, First Battle of Kharkov.

The practical use is not given: Zond 6 was itself a test flight; later skip entries (Zond 7/8, Chang'e 5-T1 2014, Chang'e 5 2020 sample return) are later.
searched: Wikipedia Zond 6, Zond 4, Apollo 4, Atmospheric entry; archive.org 1968 newspapers.

what: The Vasari Corridor, a raised passageway built for Cosimo I de' Medici in Florence, linking Palazzo Vecchio to the Uffizi and Palazzo Pitti over streets and the Ponte Vecchio.
fit: A walkway raised above the street joins upper levels of buildings so Cosimo could cross without descending.

sources.title: Vasari Corridor
sources.quote: The works were to be completed in five months, in order to commemorate the marriage of Cosimo's son, Francesco, to Johanna of Austria, in 1565.

sources.title: Skyway
sources.quote: Florence, Italy, Vasari Corridor, connects Palazzo Vecchio to Uffizi and then to Palazzo Pitti, 16th century

note: Bridge of Sighs, Venice (c. 1600) is later. Earlier medieval covered passages (such as the Passetto di Borgo, 1277) run along a wall, not across streets, and were not checked. Modern commercial skyways start with Minneapolis in 1962. Mass adoption not claimed: Minneapolis had 7 segments by 1972 but I found no sourced use measure.
searched: Wikipedia Vasari Corridor, Skyway, Minneapolis Skyway System.

sources.title: Vasari Corridor

what: Stephane Leduc of Nantes induced electric sleep with low-voltage interrupted currents, first in rabbits and dogs and then on himself in 1902 (published 1903).
fit: An apparatus (interrupter-driven current through head electrodes) that puts the subject into tranquil sleep matches a device that induces sleep.

sources.title: Scientific American Supplement 1907-02-23: Vol 63 Iss 1625
sources.quote: Prof. Leduc first submitted himself to experiment in 1902.

note: Leduc's state was closer to electro-anesthesia than restful sleep, and he did not claim a restful-sleep therapy; rejected nothing earlier. Hypnotic drugs (chloral hydrate 1869) are not apparatus and were not counted. Sleep spray/gas not found.
searched: archive.org full text for electric sleep Leduc 1900-1965; Wikipedia Electrosleep (no page text found).

what: By 1948 electric sleep (electronarcosis) was being applied to psychiatric patients in the US, Canada and Britain as prolonged sleep therapy; Soviet clinics (Gilyarovsky, Livenstev) developed 'electrosleep' for neuroses in the same period.
fit: Patients with mental disturbance were put to sleep and kept asleep by an electric apparatus to calm them, matching a device used to induce soothing sleep.

sources.title: Coronet 1948-03: Vol 23
sources.quote: Today doctors in many parts of the U.S., Canada and Britain are applying both methods in cases of mental dis

note: The date is the latest the magazine proves; the true first clinical use may be a year or two earlier and is not pinned down. Popular article, not a medical paper. Leduc's 1900s work was experimental.
searched: archive.org full text for electric sleep 1948-1956 and Soviet monograph Elektroson (DTIC ADA354482, undated first edition).

what: Zust et al. (University of Bern) played recorded pseudoword/German word pairs to young adults in slow-wave sleep and found they had formed and kept new word associations that showed up on an implicit test after waking.
fit: Recorded vocabulary was played to sleeping people and they retained new verbal associations from it, so teaching by recorded sound during sleep worked, though only for implicit word-pair associations and not for general lessons.

sources.title: Implicit Vocabulary Learning during Sleep Is Bound to Slow-Wave Peaks
sources.quote: While in slow-wave sleep during a nap, a series of word pairs comprising pseudowords, e.g., "tofer," and actual German words, e.g., "Haus" (house), were played

note: Second pass gave nothing. This is the earliest strictly fitting result I found. Rejected: Saliger's Psycho-Phone (1927, patented 1932, sold as a sleep-teaching phonograph) and 1950s-60s commercial sleep-learning records, because there was no evidence they worked (the Wikipedia history says Emmons and Simon's 1956 EEG studies found material presented during sleep was not recalled and called it 'impractical and probably impossible'); Arzi et al. 2012 (Nature Neuroscience, 'Humans can learn new information during sleep') showed learning of tone-odour associations in sleep, which is conditioning rather than teaching with lessons, so earlier but a loose analogue; Schreiner and Rasch 2015 only cued words learned while awake. Hypnosis tapes: no controlled evidence found. The abstract itself says earlier evidence 'is inconclusive'. Hence low confidence.
searched: Wikipedia Sleep learning; Crossref for Zust 2019, Arzi 2012, Emmons/Simon 1955-56; Semantic Scholar abstract for Zust 2019 (Arzi abstract not returned); no archive.org full-text search made for 1950s sleep-learning newspapers.
check_note: checker proposed 1942-07 (Lawrence LeShan (College of William and Mary) played a phonograph record of 'My finger nails taste terribly bitter' to 2); rejected in review: The checker's replacement, LeShan's 1942 nail-biting study, played a suggestion rather than a lesson, did not establish that the boys were asleep, and was not borne out once sleep was measured (Emmons and Simon 1956, cited in the checker's own note), so it does not show that teaching during sleep works. The 2019 milestone stays.

what: The U.S. Army fired a Davy Crockett M388 round with a W54 nuclear warhead from a recoilless gun 1.7 miles away in the Little Feller I shot at the Nevada Test Site (the warhead was first tested on 7 July 1962 in Little Feller II).
fit: A nuclear warhead small enough for an infantry crew was launched from a recoilless smoothbore gun and detonated, the definition's recoilless-rifle case.

sources.title: Davy Crockett (nuclear device)
sources.quote: actual firing of the Davy Crockett from a distance of 1.7 miles (2.7 km) in the Little Feller I test shot on July 17, 1962

note: Earlier lab-style small devices (Gnat, Scarab) are research designs, not weapons. The 280 mm atomic cannon (1953) was artillery and not carried by infantry. The warhead alone was tested on 1962-07-07, which does not show the delivery system working. Possible earlier tests of the W54 warhead in the 1950s were not found.
searched: Wikipedia Davy Crockett (nuclear device), W54, Atomic demolition munition.

what: Generra Sportswear of Seattle launched Hypercolor T-shirts and shorts in 1991, using a Matsui thermochromic pigment so the garment changes color with the wearer's body heat and the air temperature.
fit: The fabric itself senses heat and responds by changing color, matching the definition's color-changing, environment- and wearer-responsive garments.

sources.title: Hypercolor
sources.quote: The shirts were produced with several color change choices beginning in 1991.

note: Electrically heated gloves with a heat regulator were reported in Scientific American in June 1912 and electrically heated flying suits were used in the 1940s, but their heating was switched or rheostat-set by the user and did not sense and respond to wearer or environment, so I treated them as loose analogues. I did not find an earlier working thermochromic garment; thermostat-controlled heated clothing might be earlier and was not dated.
searched: archive.org full text for electrically heated clothing/gloves/suits, thermostat heated suit, thermochromic garments, Hypercolor Generra; Wikipedia Hypercolor.

what: Hypercolor garments went on sale to the public in 1991 as ordinary clothing.
fit: Sold and worn as real garments that change color with heat.

sources.title: Hypercolor
sources.quote: The shirts were produced with several color change choices beginning in 1991.

note: Product launch is both demonstration and first use; see first_demonstration.
searched: see first_demonstration.

what: Hypercolor was a youth fashion fad across the United States in 1991-1992; a 1992 trade article says the sportswear was so hot the maker struggled to keep up with orders.
fit: Ordinary teens bought and wore color-changing garments routinely during the fad.

sources.title: HP Professional Vol. 06 No. 04 Apr, 1992
sources.quote: Hypercolor sportswear is hot.

note: It was a short-lived fad (washing destroyed the effect), so mass adoption is arguable; no durable, routine category of smart clothing was found, so I tied it to the fad year.
searched: see first_demonstration.

what: Corning Glass Works (Armistead and Stookey) published photochromic silicate glass in Science in April 1964: glass with silver halide crystals that darkens in ultraviolet light and clears again.
fit: A glass whose visible transmission changes automatically in response to light, with clear-state transmission about that of window glass, matching the definition's glass that changes opacity or filters in response to light.

sources.title: Photochromic Silicate Glasses Sensitized by Silver Halides
sources.quote: Photochromic Silicate Glasses Sensitized by Silver Halides

sources.title: Review of Research on Flash Blindness, Chorioretinal Burns, Countermeasures, and Related Topics
sources.quote: transmission of photochromic glass is essentially that of window glass

note: This is the first light-responsive window-type glass I could verify. Electrochromic tungsten oxide films (Deb, 1969-1973) and Land's 1930s polarizer light-valve patents are later or only patents; I found no dated 1930s working polarizing window. The photochromic material was first sold as eyeglass lenses (1960s), a loose fit for 'window', so confidence is low.
searched: Wikipedia Smart glass, Photochromic lens, Electrochromism; Crossref for Armistead and Stookey; archive.org full text for polaroid window, photochromic glass windows 1930-1968.

what: Nippon Sheet Glass launched UMU, the first switchable light control glass that goes between transparent and opaque when voltage is switched, in 1987.
fit: A glass pane that changes opacity electrically on command, for use as window glass.

sources.title: Smart glass
sources.quote: In 1987, Nippon Sheet Glass (NSG) launched UMU, the first switchable light control glass.

note: Earlier electrically switchable glass products (liquid crystal or SPD) were not found; photochromic glass products of the 1960s were lenses. No mass_adoption: smart glass windows remain a niche or premium product (aircraft, offices) rather than routine for ordinary people.
searched: Wikipedia Smart glass history section.

what: Westinghouse engineer Jim Sutherland's home-built ECHO IV computer, running household functions in his house, was made public.

sources.title: ECHO IV
sources.quote: It was made public for the first time in 1966.

note: Considered earlier appliance automation (1900s electric appliances, Monsanto House of the Future 1957) but those were not machines responding to occupants under computer control. ECHO IV is the earliest house run by a computer found; the exact 1966 date (April per CHM) rests on a secondary source and the CHM page could not be fetched.

what: ECHO IV served the Sutherland household's daily routines in his home through 1976.

sources.title: ECHO IV
sources.quote: The computer was working in the Sutherland's house until 1976, and was donated to the Computer Museum in Boston in 1984.

note: Same event as the demonstration; it was a one-off home-built prototype in real daily use for about a decade. No earlier real-household use found.

what: At the Battle of Macau the Dutch fired a barrel of damp gunpowder into the wind so their landing party could come ashore under cover of smoke.
fit: Smoke was made on purpose to hide an advancing landing force from defenders, the definition's function.

sources.title: Battle of Macau
sources.quote: a barrel of damp gunpowder was fired into the wind so that the Dutch could land under the cover of smoke

note: The page calls it 'one of the first recorded instances', so earlier uses may exist. Web pages claim Romans burned green vegetation and Vikings burned peat as smoke screens, with no named battle or primary source, so rejected. Cochrane's 1812 smoke-vessel proposal and the American Civil War blockade-runner smoke are later.
searched: web search on history of smoke screens; Wikipedia Smoke screen, Battle of Macau, Cochrane; fandom page refused (403).

what: The same Dutch landing at Macau was a real attack carried out under an artificial smoke cover.
fit: Troops were hidden by artificially made smoke during a real operation.

sources.title: Battle of Macau
sources.quote: a barrel of damp gunpowder was fired into the wind so that the Dutch could land under the cover of smoke

note: Demonstration and use coincide: this was a use in war. The Portuguese defenders shot into the smoke, so it concealed the landing only in part.
searched: Wikipedia Battle of Macau.

what: U.S. Army ordnance captain Alfred Mordecai tested Schonbein's gun-cotton as a charge in a musket and reported that its combustion is unattended with smoke.
fit: A nitrocellulose charge propelled a bullet from a gun with no visible smoke, the definition's mechanism and function.

sources.title: Journal of the Franklin Institute 1846-12: Vol 12 Iss 6
sources.quote: The combustion of the gun-cotton is unattended with smoke

note: Gun-cotton was unstable and not a usable service propellant, but the test shows a smokeless charge working in a gun. Later candidates: Schultze powder (patented 1863, described in 1865 as giving transparent gases), Poudre B (Vieille, 1884). Gunpowder-era 'low smoke' claims were not found. The Anglo-American 1846-11-21 said a slight vapor, not smoke, is given off.
searched: archive.org full text for gun-cotton and smoke 1846-1848, Schultze powder 1864-1868; Wikipedia Smokeless powder, Nitrocellulose.

what: France adopted the Lebel Model 1886 rifle, the first military firearm to use smokeless powder (Vieille's Poudre B), which entered service in 1887.
fit: Army rifles were loaded with a nitrocellulose propellant that gave almost no smoke.

sources.title: Lebel Model 1886 rifle
sources.quote: The Lebel rifle has the distinction of being the first military firearm to use smokeless powder ammunition.

note: Earlier non-military use is possible: Schultze wood powder was sold from the mid-1860s for sporting guns and Austrian artillery tried Lenk's gun-cotton in the 1860s, but I found no source of actual use. The 1886 date is the rifle's model year; the service entry is 1887.
searched: Wikipedia Lebel Model 1886 rifle, Smokeless powder.

what: John Mullaly's steam snow melter, a railway car with boiler and steam chamber that melted snow from street-railway tracks, was tried on the Lexington Avenue railway in New York.
fit: A machine melted snow in place by discharging steam on it so that tracks stayed clear, one of the melting-machine forms the definition lists.

sources.title: A Steam Snow Melter
sources.quote: was lately tried here on the Lexington avenue railway

sources.title: A Steam Snow Melter
sources.quote: is there discharged directly upon the snow be- neath, which is instantly melted

note: Earlier snow-melting devices might exist (I searched archive.org periodicals 1840-1900 and found this earliest hit). Later: 1902 New York snow-melting automobile, 1930s railway switch snow-melting oil, 1940s embedded hot-water pipe pavements (Welding Engineer 1947). Heated-pavement and sidewalk systems were not found earlier than the 1940s in my searches.
searched: archive.org full text 'snow melting', 'snow melter' 1860-1947; Wikipedia Snow melter.

what: UNIVAC I, used by CBS on election night, predicted an Eisenhower landslide from 5.5% of the vote.

sources.title: UNIVAC I
sources.quote: The fifth machine (built for the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission) was used by CBS to predict the result of the 1952 presidential election.

note: Earlier computer forecasts not found. Statistical model of people, as definition requires; the machine was off on the first try, but the 442 vs 438 electoral vote result was close.

what: Same broadcast: the forecast was used on live television for the real election.

sources.title: UNIVAC I
sources.quote: On election night, Eisenhower received 34,075,029 votes in a 442–89 Electoral College victory. UNIVAC had a margin of error of 3.5%

note: Same event as the demonstration. Computerized predictions then became a widely used part of election night broadcasts, but no dated source for mass adoption.

what: Bernard Lyot, working at the Pic du Midi observatory in summer 1930, used his coronagraph (an occulting disc and baffled optics) to obtain the first definite record of coronal light outside a total solar eclipse.
fit: This is the observation of the corona outside a total eclipse that the definition asks for; the nature of the corona as hot ionized gas is dated in the note.

sources.publisher: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
sources.title: Monthly Notices RAS 1931-02-13, vol 91 no 4
sources.quote: he has secured the first definite photographic record of coronal light outside a total eclipse

sources.title: Coronagraph
sources.quote: The coronagraph was introduced in 1931 by the French astronomer Bernard Lyot

note: Rejected: Huggins 1883 and Hale 1890s attempts to photograph the corona without an eclipse (reported as unsuccessful in the 1933 MNRAS notice 'To Lyot is due the credit for the first success'). The explanation half: Grotrian 1939 and Edlen 1940-41 identified the coronal lines as highly ionized iron in million-degree gas (not radiation-driven particles or coronium), so the 'radiation-driven particle' explanation in the definition was not the finding. I dated only the observation outside an eclipse; no separate practical-use milestone claimed (coronagraphs became routine observatory tools in the 1930s).
searched: archive.org scanned MNRAS/Science News Letter 1931-33; Wikipedia Coronagraph, Bernard Lyot, Solar corona.

what: NASA Lewis engineers activated a photovoltaic system at Schuchuli village on the Papago reservation in Arizona, the first solar electric village.
fit: Photovoltaic arrays converted sunlight into electricity that powered a village's buildings (small scale, 3.5 kW).

sources.title: NASA Lewis Designed the First Solar Electric Village
sources.quote: On December 16, 1978 engineers from NASA’s Lewis Research Center activated a new photovoltaic system

sources.title: Social and Economic Impact of Solar Electricity at Schuchuli Village
sources.quote: Social and Economic Impact of Solar Electricity at Schuchuli Village

note: Considered: Bell Labs 1954 silicon cell (a device, not a power system for buildings), Vanguard 1 1958 (satellite), Francia's Sant'Ilario concentrating plant near Genoa (1965 or 1968 per conflicting sources; electric output not verified), Arco's 1 MWp Lugo PV park (end of 1982, larger scale but later).
searched: Wikipedia Solar cell, Timeline of solar cells, Photovoltaic power station, CSP; NASA history and NTRS.

what: The Schuchuli system supplied the village with daily household electricity.
fit: Solar electricity was used routinely for its real purpose, powering homes in a remote village.

sources.title: NASA Lewis Designed the First Solar Electric Village
sources.quote: On December 16, 1978 engineers from NASA’s Lewis Research Center activated a new photovoltaic system

note: Same event; Lugo 1982 is the first 1 MWp solar park (Wikipedia: Photovoltaic power station).
searched: as above

what: JAXA's IKAROS, launched 2010-05-20, deployed its 14 m square polyimide sail on 2010-06-10 in interplanetary space and was pushed by sunlight, confirmed by acceleration measurements; it flew past Venus in December 2010.
fit: A spacecraft was propelled by sunlight pressure on a large thin sail, as in the definition.

sources.title: Aerospace America July-August 2010
sources.quote: Pressure exerted by photons—minute “packages” of light energy emitted by the Sun—are now pushing the sail along

sources.title: IKAROS
sources.quote: IKAROS is the first spacecraft to successfully demonstrate solar sail technology in interplanetary space

note: Rejected: Mariner 10 (1974-75) and MESSENGER used solar pressure on panels for attitude control only; Znamya 2 (1993) a reflector deployed from Mir, not propulsion; Cosmos 1 (2005) failed to reach orbit; NanoSail-D2 (2011) and LightSail 2 (2019) are later. No first_practical_use: IKAROS and later sails are technology demonstrators; mass adoption has not occurred.
searched: Wikipedia IKAROS, Solar sail; archive.org Aerospace America 2010.

what: Augustin Mouchot's solar boiler drove a small steam engine, shown to Napoleon III in 1866 and working at Biarritz.
fit: A mirror concentrated sunlight on a boiler and the steam drove an engine.

sources.title: Another Solar Engine
sources.quote: the machine was taken thither and the ex- periment succeeded

note: Source appeared 2 years 4 months after the event, so it is a reference. Mouchot built a solar boiler in 1864 (same source) and the Emperor saw it on 2 September 1866 but weather interrupted it; success followed at Biarritz. Pifre's 1882 solar printing press (Nature, 21 Sept 1882) was later. Salomon de Caus-style proposals were designs, not working engines.
searched: archive.org Scientific American 1869, Nature 1882; Wikipedia Mouchot.

what: Frank Shuman's 50-55 horsepower sun-power plant at Maadi near Cairo pumped Nile water for irrigation.
fit: Mirror troughs heated a boiler whose steam drove an engine doing real pumping work.

sources.publisher: Transactions of the third International Congress of Tropical Agriculture (Shuman)
sources.title: The Utilization of Sun Power for Irrigation and Other Purposes in Tropical Agriculture
sources.quote: have erected a 5O-h.p. sun-power plant at Maadi, a suburb of Cairo, in Egypt

sources.title: Frank Shuman
sources.quote: Shuman built the world’s first solar thermal power station in Maadi, Egypt (1912-1913).

note: Pifre 1882 solar printing press and Mouchot's cookers and distillers were earlier uses but demonstration-scale; Eneas Pasadena 1901 not verified. Mass adoption: Solar One (1981-82, 10 MW) and later plants are not 'ordinary people routinely' use.
searched: Wikipedia CSP, Shuman, Mouchot; archive.org searches 1866-1915.

what: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center researchers designed, built and tested a direct-gain solar thermal rocket engine in a ground test facility using about 10 kW of concentrated sunlight to heat hydrogen propellant.
fit: A ground engine heated hydrogen with concentrated sunlight through a mirror concentrator and expanded it through a nozzle to produce thrust, per the definition.

sources.publisher: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center image record (Internet Archive)
sources.title: Solar Thermal Propulsion Test Facility
sources.quote: have designed, fabricated, and tested the first solar thermal engine

note: NASA's caption claims 'first' but earlier US Air Force Rocket Propulsion Laboratory work exists (1980s solar furnace tests with hydrogen to about 1810 K; Electro-Optical Systems 1963 absorber at about 2300 K) and I could not fetch a page showing measured thrust (DTIC and ADS refused), so the date may be too late. No flight demonstration exists (the Shooting Star and ISUS flights were not flown); the JHU/APL helium proof of concept was 2020. No first_practical_use or mass adoption.
searched: WebSearch, NTRS API (solar thermal propulsion), Wikipedia Solar thermal rocket, archive.org metadata for MSFC-9906910.

what: French Anderson, Michael Blaese and Kenneth Culver began the first therapeutic gene transfer trial at NIH, treating Ashanthi DeSilva (ADA-SCID) with her own gene-modified T cells.
fit: Genes were inserted into the cells of an already-born patient to change her body's function, matching direct manipulation of genes or living cells in a living person.

sources.title: Gene therapy
sources.quote: the first gene therapy widely accepted as a success was demonstrated in a trial that started on 14 September 1990

note: Earlier candidates: the May 1989 NIH gene-marking trial (Rosenberg) inserted a marker gene into TIL cells with no therapeutic effect, so not a body-reshaping manipulation; Martin Cline's unauthorized 1980 attempts did not work. No contemporary source fetched (Science and NEJM refuse scripted access).
searched: Wikipedia Gene therapy.

what: China's SFDA approved Gendicine (recombinant adenovirus p53) for head and neck cancer, the first approved gene therapy product.
fit: A marketed treatment that delivers a gene into the cells of existing patients to alter their cell behavior fits manipulating genes in an already-born person.

sources.title: Gendicine
sources.quote: Gendicine was the first gene therapy product to obtain regulatory approval for clinical use in humans

note: Clinical-trial use since 1990 is experimental; Strimvelis (EU 2016) and Luxturna (US 2017) followed. Gendicine's efficacy is disputed, but it was approved and sold.
searched: Wikipedia Gendicine and Gene therapy.

what: On the US revenue cutter Miami's first ice patrol cruise (15 April to 1 May 1914), Reginald Fessenden and R. Fulton Blake used the Fessenden oscillator to get an echo from a large iceberg.
fit: An instrument that detects an obstacle (an iceberg) by the echo of underwater sound, matching the definition's mechanism and function.

sources.title: The Fessenden Oscillator Obtains an Echo from Iceberg
sources.quote: The Fessenden Oscillator Obtains an Echo from Iceberg.

sources.title: Sonar
sources.quote: In that test, Fessenden demonstrated depth sounding, underwater communications (Morse code) and echo ranging, detecting an iceberg at a 2-mile (3.2 km) range.

note: Candidates rejected: Lewis Fry Richardson's 1912 echo-ranging patent and Alexander Behm's 1913 echo-sounder patent (patents, no working demonstration found); Fessenden's earlier 1912-1913 Boston Harbor tests (experimental, the iceberg echo is the best-documented working result); Langevin and Chilowsky's WWI ultrasonic work (1915-1918) came later.
searched: Wikipedia Sonar and Echo sounding; archive.org full text for Fessenden iceberg echo (Scientific American 1914).

what: Dr. H. C. Hayes of the US Navy finished the sonic depth finder in June 1922 and the destroyer USS Stewart used it on its voyage from Newport to Gibraltar and on to Manila, followed by the first bathymetric surveys of the Pacific coast.
fit: A ship-mounted instrument that finds the sea floor depth by underwater sound echoes, used for its real purpose at sea.

sources.title: Make First Contour Map of Ocean Bed
sources.quote: Successful tests were made and excellent results were obtained with this apparatus by the U. S. S. Stewart on a voyage from Newport

note: Earlier operational claims (Fessenden oscillators on British H-class submarines in 1915 were for signaling, not echo detection; Behm's Echolot was sold in the early 1920s) were not verified with dated sources, so the date could be a year or two earlier. Mass adoption not claimed: routine use on ships and by anglers (fish finders) came later but no verified source was found.
searched: archive.org full text for echo sounding and sonic depth finder 1913-1923.

what: Robert W. Wood and Alfred Loomis published experiments with a powerful quartz ultrasonic oscillator (100 to 700 kHz) in which small fish and frogs were killed by one or two minutes of exposure, confirming what Paul Langevin had seen at Toulon in World War I.
fit: A high-intensity ultrasonic beam from a device was shown to kill and injure living animals.

sources.title: The Physical and Biological Effects of High-frequency Sound-waves of Great Intensity
sources.quote: Small fish and frogs are killed by an exposure of one or two minutes, an observation also made by Langevin at Toulon

sources.title: Robert W. Wood
sources.quote: fish would be killed or an experimenter's hand would suffer searing pain if placed in the path of an intense sound beam

note: A lab effect, not built as a weapon; I count it because the definition asks for a device using high-intensity ultrasound to injure or kill, and I found no sonic device built as a weapon before it. Langevin's own observation (about 1917 to 1918) is earlier but has no dated source; the 1927 paper recounts it. Rejected: the Stuka siren (Larmgerat) of 1937 to 1939, a ram-air siren meant to scare, which is only loosely a sonic weapon; Gavreau's 1960s infrasound tests are later; the Nazi 'sonic cannon' (Wallauschek) is a wartime report and did not work as a weapon.
searched: Wikipedia Sonic weapon, Long Range Acoustic Device, Robert W. Wood, Jericho trumpet/Ju 87; archive.org full text for Wood and Loomis 1927.

what: The cruise ship Seabourn Spirit used a long-range acoustic device (LRAD) to repel pirates who attacked it off Somalia.
fit: A focused beam of high-intensity sound was used against attackers to drive them off, the deterrent and injure-or-frighten function of the definition.

sources.title: Long Range Acoustic Device
sources.quote: the luxury cruise ship Seabourn Spirit employed an LRAD to repel pirates who attacked the vessel with rocket-propelled grenades

note: The LRAD was launched in 2003 as a hailing device; earlier military use in Iraq in 2003 or 2004 is plausible but not found in the fetched page. The page says the effect on the pirates is not completely clear. The Stuka siren of 1937 to 1939 is an older sound device meant to frighten but is loose and was not counted.
searched: Wikipedia Long Range Acoustic Device, Sonic weapon.

what: Francis Galton described in Inquiries into Human Faculty (1883) his ultrasonic whistles (devised 1876): used in the Zoological Gardens and in streets he made small dogs turn round, turned a cat's ear, and frightened a pony.
fit: A whistle sounding above human hearing that made animals respond (turning dogs, frightening a pony), matching the definition's ultrasonic whistle used to summon or terrify animals.

sources.title: Inquiries into human faculty and its development
sources.quote: I once frightened a pony with one of these whistles in the middle of a large field.

sources.title: Dog whistle
sources.quote: It was invented in 1876 by Francis Galton

note: Galton's whistle was a research instrument for testing hearing; the book dates it to a paper read in 1876 but the animal trials are undated, so I used the 1883 publication. Ordinary audible whistles, horns and herding calls for animals are far older and cannot be dated, so I took the ultrasonic whistle as the alternative to date. Fish-herding horns and underwater hums and ultrasonic rat repellers were not searched in depth.
searched: Wikipedia Dog whistle and Acme Whistles; archive.org full text for Galton's Inquiries (whistle), silent dog whistle 1884-1935.

what: By 1923 the silent dog whistle was a known working tool that calls a dog from 100 yards away without the person beside you hearing it.
fit: A whistle that calls (summons) a dog by sound beyond human hearing, used for its real purpose.

sources.title: Appleton Post-Crescent 1923-05-26
sources.quote: which calls a four-Iogg-cd friend 100 yards away yot rannol bo hr-.'ird by t h p man you aro wnlkinsr with

note: This is the earliest dated report of routine use I verified; commercial silent dog whistles were sold from the late 1800s but I could not source a date. The archive.org item labeled 'House & Garden, October 1916' with a silent whistle advertisement is a mis-dated mid-century item and was not used. what: Gemini III (Grissom and Young) flew with the IBM-built Gemini onboard digital computer, which navigated and produced reentry guidance commands for the crew.
fit: An onboard digital computer navigated the spacecraft and computed steering (bank) commands, which the crew flew, to fly the entry path to a landing target; on Gemini III it also generated the data for orbit-changing burns, so it calculates and steers, with the crew closing the loop.

sources.title: Gemini Titan 3 Press Kit
sources.quote: insert landing area parameters in the spacecraft computer, retrofire, and descend to a planned recovery area

note: Kept the second pass date (Gemini III, 23 March 1965, first crewed flight of the IBM Gemini guidance computer), now with a fetched contemporary press kit and a 1967 NASA summary. Gemini III's lift shortfall meant the crew did not follow the computer all the way, and the full onboard-computer rendezvous burns came on Gemini 6A/7 (Dec 1965); Gemini 4 (June 1965) could not use the computer for reentry after a memory alteration. Earlier candidates rejected: Mercury (1961-63; no onboard digital computer, orbits computed by ground IBM 7090s), Vostok (analog 'Globus' navigation), Atlas/Titan/Thor launch-vehicle guidance computers (1958-62) and Saturn I (1964), which steer rockets or missiles rather than a spacecraft and were mostly ground-based or not checked; submarine and ship inertial navigators (1950s, analog, no burns). The press kit only shows that a spacecraft computer existed and was loaded for the flight; the claim that it flew on Gemini III rests on the 1967 summary. Practical use is given as the same flight: it was a real mission, not a bench test, but a full 'real purpose' use (rendezvous) was Dec 1965.

note: Kept the second pass date (Gemini III, 23 March 1965, first crewed flight of the IBM Gemini guidance computer), now with a fetched contemporary press kit and a 1967 NASA summary. Gemini III's lift shortfall meant the crew did not follow the computer all the way, and the full onboard-computer rendezvous burns came on Gemini 6A/7 (Dec 1965); Gemini 4 (June 1965) could not use the computer for reentry after a memory alteration. Earlier candidates rejected: Mercury (1961-63; no onboard digital computer, orbits computed by ground IBM 7090s), Vostok (analog 'Globus' navigation), Atlas/Titan/Thor launch-vehicle guidance computers (1958-62) and Saturn I (1964), which steer rockets or missiles rather than a spacecraft and were mostly ground-based or not checked; submarine and ship inertial navigators (1950s, analog, no burns). The press kit only shows that a spacecraft computer existed and was loaded for the flight; the claim that it flew on Gemini III rests on the 1967 summary. Practical use is given as the same flight: it was a real mission, not a bench test, but a full 'real purpose' use (rendezvous) was Dec 1965.
searched: ia_search3 for Gemini 3 computer 1965-1966, Gemini Titan 3 press kit text (computer, inertial, guidance), Gemini Summary Conference text (onboard computer, Gemini III) via archive.org/NTRS; NTRS API search (no useful hits); Wikipedia Gemini Guidance Computer and Gemini 3 as in the second pass (not re-quoted). The JASA paper is dated 1952-11; the Bell Labs Record 1956 source is more than two years later, so it is a reference.

sources.quote: The first Speak & Spell was introduced at the summer Consumer Electronics Show in 1978

Speak & Spell and talking chess/bridge computers (Popular Electronics ads and reviews 1980) were bought by ordinary families years before Siri; the year is a judgment (introduction 1978, routine household use evident by 1980-81) because no sales figure could be fetched. what: RCA Laboratories (Harry Olson and Herbert Belar, Princeton) built a phonetic typewriter model that typed spoken sounds; reported in J. Acoust. Soc. Am. in 1956 and confirmed by RCA to the press in August 1956.
fit: A machine listens to speech and types the words automatically, as a single-talker laboratory model with a small vocabulary.

sources.publisher: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America (Crossref record)
sources.title: Phonetic Typewriter
sources.quote: a simplified model of a phonetic typewriter has been developed incorporating all of these aspects

sources.title: The Atlanta Constitution, 2 August 1956
sources.quote: is a phonetic typewriter using an electronic brain to memorize words

sources.title: Challenge August-September 1956
sources.quote: developed a model of such a voice-operated typewriter which is 80 per cent accurate

note: Replaces the second pass (Kyoto Sonotype 1961). Earlier candidates: Steno-Sonograph (Electronics, Sept 1950; fetched) prints visual sound characters for a human stenographer to read and 'is not yet perfected', so no text output, rejected; Typo-Sonograph in the same article was only under construction; Bell Labs 1952 digit recognizer (Audrey) recognizes ten spoken digits, not dictation text. Date 1956-07 is the JASA record date (the abstract appeared in the 1956 volume; full paper Nov 1956); Kyoto 1960-61 and Tangora 1980s are later.
searched: ia_search3 for 'phonetic typewriter' 1950-1958 (found JASA 1956, Challenge 1956, Acoustical Engineering 1957, Wisdom 1956, Atlanta Constitution); page_text3 on Electronics 1950-09 (Steno-Sonograph); Crossref JASA records. Pre-1950 typing-from-speech machines not searched separately.

what: Kurzweil Applied Intelligence officially released its 1,000-word Voicerad system in Boston in December 1986; a radiologist was already writing his reports with it by voice. Dragon Systems had announced Voicescribe-1000 'automatic dictation transcription system' in June 1986.
fit: A computer listens to a user's spoken dictation of reports and produces the edited, printed text, used by a working radiologist.

sources.title: Voice system cures MD ills
sources.quote: allows radiologists to dictate, edit and print out diagnostic X-ray reports by voice

sources.title: Speech transcriber announced

Earlier: Threshold Technology voice input from 1972 was data entry of commands, not dictation; Kurzweil 1985 Voice Report not found in searches. Voicescribe-1000 was only announced in June 1986 (availability not shown), so Voicerad December 1986 is the first documented in use. Limited vocabulary and discrete speech, so a strict dictation fit but narrow.

what: A Bell Laboratories sound spectrograph (R. K. Potter and colleagues) was demonstrated to the National Defense Research Committee, turning speech into a visible pattern.
fit: The device converts speech into a visible frequency-time-intensity pattern that can be read.

what: Bell Laboratories visible speech instruments (sound spectrograph, cathode ray translator) were in use in an educational research program for the deaf.

what: Manel Torres's Fabrican spray-on fabric (polymers and fibers sprayed from a gun or aerosol can that dries to a non-woven fabric on skin or other surfaces) was shown at London Fashion Week in 2010.
fit: A spray that dries on contact into a thin clothing-like fabric on skin, matching the 'spray-on clothing' alternative; it is not shown to shield against cold, heat or weather.

sources.title: Fabrican
sources.quote: Fabrican was showcased at London Fashion Week 2010 as well as in fashion shows in Milan and Moscow and at TED Talks.

note: Considered and left out as loose: spray-on plastic wound dressings (for example SCAN Spray-On Wound Dressing, Health Forum, 1960-10, and others in Hospital Topics 1955-1961), which dry to a protective film on skin but are medical dressings, not protection against weather or clothing; collodion and liquid bandages (19th century) likewise; wartime spray-on 'cocoon' plastic coatings for equipment were not checked and are not body coatings. The Fabrican date may be earlier (company founded 2003) but the first public showing I could source is 2010.
searched: Wikipedia Fabrican; archive.org full text for plastic spray skin, spray-on plastic bandage 1940-1965.

what: The first Zeiss Model I planetarium projector showed the night sky on a 16 m dome on the roof of the Zeiss works in Jena.
fit: An instrument projected the star field onto a dome, showing the night sky (from varying latitudes, not from other stars).

fit: The projector displayed the night sky to the public.

sources.title: Planetarium

fit: Government controlled radio and receivers were provided so official messages reached all citizens.

what: The Central Railroad of New Jersey put an ALCO diesel-electric boxcab switcher into service at its Bronx waterfront terminal, an early replacement of steam switchers by a newer power source.

note: Earlier electrification displaced steam in places (Baltimore Belt Line tunnel 1895, Wikipedia 'first mainline railroad electrification in the United States'; New York's Kaufman Act of 1923) but no source states steam engines were replaced there. what: Henri Giffard flew a steam-driven, propeller-and-rudder hydrogen airship 27 km from Paris to Elancourt, making turns and circles.

what: Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton showed in deep-sea sediment cores that Earth's ice-age cycles track periodic shifts in its orbit (eccentricity, tilt, precession).
fit: Establishes that a habitable planet (Earth) swings between glacial and warm climate because its orbit and axis shift, which is the orbit-shift alternative of the definition.

sources.title: Variations in the Earth's Orbit: Pacemaker of the Ice Ages
sources.quote: changes in the earth's orbital geometry are the fundamental cause of the succession of Quaternary ice ages

sources.title: Milankovitch cycles
sources.quote: a seminal paper by Hays, Imbrie, and Shackleton provide additional validation through physical evidence

note: Dated the orbit-shift alternative on Earth. Earlier candidates: Croll (1860s) and Milankovitch (1920s-40s) hypotheses, rejected as proposals, not established; Agassiz-era glaciation discovery shows ice ages but not their cause. Variable-star and twin-sun climate swings on another habitable planet have not been observed, so those alternatives are not dated.
searched: Crossref/Wikipedia for Milankovitch cycles and Hays 1976; WebSearch not needed further.

what: Yasumitsu Aoki at Nemoto & Co. (Japan) developed strontium aluminate phosphors that absorb light and glow for hours; Matsuzawa et al. published SrAl2O4:Eu,Dy in 1996.

sources.quote: discovery by Yasumitsu Aoki (Nemoto & Co.) of materials with luminance approximately 10 times greater than zinc sulfide

sources.quote: A New Long Phosphorescent Phosphor with High Brightness

note: Earlier candidates rejected as too dim and short for steady illumination: Bologna stone (barium sulfide, 1602-03), Sidot zinc sulfide (1866) and ZnS:Cu watch/sign paints (1930s), which glow weakly for under an hour. Radium and promethium paints are not sunlight-charged. Date is the Wikipedia 1993 discovery; the dated contemporary paper is 1996.

sources.quote: the first demonstration that laser-induced filaments—formed in the sky by short and intense laser pulses—can guide lightning discharges over considerable distances

note: Rejected: Franklin lightning rod (1752), a passive conductor, not deflecting a strike; Project Cirrus hurricane seeding of 13 Oct 1947 (Wikipedia: first attempt to modify a hurricane), whose effect on the storm was never established and which seeded clouds rather than using a steering device; Project Stormfury (1960s), likewise unproven. what: German mine surveyor Ludger Mintrop devised a mechanical seismograph in 1914 and successfully used it to detect salt domes in Germany.
fit: An instrument using artificial seismic waves to locate buried structures (salt domes) in rock and record them, matching the definition's function with a different mechanism than a ray.

sources.title: Reflection seismology
sources.quote: a mechanical seismograph in 1914 that he successfully used to detect salt domes in Germany

note: Rejected as earlier: Schlumberger's 1912 idea of electrical prospecting for ore (bathtub tests, not a field demonstration I could date); the 1910 Leimbach and Lowy and 1926 Hulsenbeck ground-radar patents (patents only); Stern's 1929 radar sounding of a glacier (ice, not ground or rock, and later). Magnetic dip needles for ore (long before) detect rather than image, so were left out. Muon tomography of pyramid chambers (1960s-70s) is later.
searched: Wikipedia Ground-penetrating radar, Reflection seismology, Conrad Schlumberger; archive.org full text for Mintrop seismograph.

what: Mintrop's company Seismos, hired for seismic exploration in Texas and Mexico, made the first commercial discovery of oil (the Orchard salt dome, Texas) using the refraction seismic method in 1924.
fit: A seismic instrument survey used commercially to find a buried structure holding oil, the real purpose.

sources.title: Reflection seismology
sources.quote: resulting in the first commercial discovery of oil using the refraction seismic method in 1924

note: Earlier commercial salt-dome surveys in Germany after 1914 are plausible but undated in my sources. No mass_adoption claimed: ground-penetrating radar became affordable in 1975 but is used by specialists.
searched: see first_demonstration.

what: Maurin and Zötl poured dye into the Argostoli sinkholes (katavothres) on Kefalonia, Greece, and it emerged 14 days later at the Karavomylos springs near Sami, proving seawater flows through underground passages across the island.
fit: Seawater enters natural subterranean channels from the sea and runs underground to emerge at the sea on the other side of the island, matching 'natural channels carrying sea water from the sea to underground regions'.

sources.title: Karavomilos
sources.quote: The connection of Argostoli Sinkholes with Karavomilos springs was certified by Maurin & Zötl in 1963, after pouring uranium dye in the Sinkholes

note: Natural alternative dated. The sinkholes were known earlier (a mill was built on the inflow in the 1830s) but the underground link was not proven until the 1963 tracing. No built subterranean channel linking seas exists (Suez and Panama canals are open cuts; proposed Red Sea-Dead Sea pipelines are unbuilt). The source is a hydrology web page that cites the original work; the original paper was not fetched.
searched: Web search; fetched addicted2h2o.com; Wikipedia Melissani Cave.

what: Steam railways in New York, Philadelphia, Boston and Chicago began carrying people daily from outlying suburbs into the city on reduced 'commuted' fares.
fit: Cheap, fast rail let people live outside the city and travel to work daily, the first separation of home and workplace by transport.

sources.title: Commuting
sources.quote: in the 1840s, the railways engendered suburbs from which travelers paid a reduced or 'commuted' fare into the city

note: Wikipedia dates the origin only to 'the 1840s', so 1840 is the start of that decade, not a measured date. Rejected: the Brooklyn steam ferry (1814) commuter town, which crossed a river within one urban area rather than linking cities by fast transport; London's Metropolitan Railway (1863), later.
searched: Wikipedia Commuting, Commuter town, Suburb, Suburbanization; no contemporary scan checked.

what: In the US 1950 was the first year more people lived in suburbs than elsewhere, with automobile commuting routine (Levittown, 1947-51).
fit: Mass suburban living tied to automobile and rail commuting is the sprawl-from-transport outcome the definition describes.

sources.title: Suburb
sources.quote: In the U.S., 1950 was the first year that more people lived in suburbs than elsewhere.

note: Rail commuter suburbs existed from the 1840s but were a minority; 1950 is the US crossover year. Other countries (UK interwar Metroland, Japan) reached this at other dates.
searched: Wikipedia Suburb, Levittown, Commuting.

what: NASA Ames (Charles Jorgensen) announced a system that reads silent speech from throat sensors; press release dated March 17, 2004.
fit: Sensors on the throat pick up silent speech nerve signals and convert them to words.

sources.title: Subvocal recognition
sources.quote: Bluck, John (March 17, 2004). "NASA Press Release". NASA.

note: Sugie and Tsunoda (Japan, 1985) used surface EMG to tell Japanese vowels from silent speech and may be earlier, but I could not fetch a source. Throat microphones (WWII) pick up audible sound, so rejected. The quote only proves the press release exists.
searched: Wikipedia, web search (NASA page 404)

what: Stanford researchers (Hawkes and colleagues) published human climbing of vertical glass using hand-held gecko-inspired dry adhesive pads in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface, January 2015.
fit: Hand-worn adhesive pads that let a person climb a vertical glass wall by clinging, matching the definition's clinging gloves that grip walls (hand-held paddles rather than shoes or gloves).

sources.quote: Human climbing with efficiently scaled gecko-inspired dry adhesives

note: The search for earlier working suction-cup or adhesive climbing gear for people (window cleaning, military, entertainment) found only fiction (a 1968 novel) and a 1961 weightlessness study of suction cup shoes for walking in zero gravity, which is not climbing. Earlier gecko-inspired robots (Stickybot, 2006) climb but are not gear worn by people. The earlier unsourced possibility of a 1930s-1960s suction-cup climbing device was not found in dated sources, so the date may be too late.

what: Hans Bethe's 'Energy Production in Stars' (Physical Review, 1 March 1939) worked out the proton-proton chain and carbon-nitrogen cycle as the nuclear sources of stellar energy.
fit: Establishes that stars shine by converting matter through nuclear fusion into radiant energy over very long times, matching the definition's atomic-process mechanism.

sources.title: Energy Production in Stars
sources.quote: Energy Production in Stars

note: Earlier candidates: Eddington 1920 proposed hydrogen-to-helium fusion as the source (a hypothesis, not established); Atkinson and Houtermans 1929 computed reaction rates; Rutherford/Joly radioactivity ideas c. 1903 were refuted. searched: Wikipedia Stellar nucleosynthesis, Arthur Eddington; Crossref.

what: Motorized revolving house models on a turntable (a button in each room starts an electric motor that turns the house toward the sun or breeze) were shown at a Home Exposition in Nice and at the Exposition of Building and Household Arts in Paris, reported in March 1932.
fit: A building on a turntable turned by an electric motor so any room faces the sun or breeze, matching the definition's dwelling on a pivot that turns rooms toward the sun.

sources.quote: starts an electric motor which revolves the house so that the breeze or the sun is available for any room desired

note: The 1932 article says only 'not long ago', so 1931 is my estimate of the exposition year (the true date is 1932 or earlier). Villa Girasole (Marcellise, Italy), designed from 1929 and begun 1931, was finished in 1935 and is a full-size house, so it is later than the exposition models unless its first turn came earlier. A 1927 Electrical Review item on a 'revolving house' was a lighting-lecture room display, not a dwelling.
searched: archive.org full text for revolving house, house revolves follow the sun, 1880-1935; Wikipedia Villa Girasole.

fit: A full-size dwelling on a rotating base driven by motors that turns to follow the sun, used as a real home.

what: A team of eleven geologists (Mortimer et al.) concluded in GSA Today that Zealandia, an almost entirely submerged mass of continental crust that subsided after leaving Gondwana, fulfills all requirements to be a continent.
fit: A continent-scale landmass that subsided beneath the sea (about 94 percent submerged), leaving New Zealand and New Caledonia as remnants, matches 'vast land that sank leaving remnants'.

sources.title: Zealandia: Earth’s Hidden Continent
sources.quote: Zealandia: Earth’s Hidden Continent

sources.title: Zealandia
sources.quote: a team of eleven geologists from New Zealand, New Caledonia, and Australia concluded that Zealandia fulfills all the requirements to be considered a submerged continent

note: Only a scientifically real submerged continent counts; Atlantis and Lemuria were never confirmed (no ruins found), and Lemuria as a sunken Indian Ocean continent was refuted by plate tectonics. Earlier: Luyendyk coined/proposed Zealandia in 1995 and Mortimer and Campbell argued it in a 2014 book, but 2017 is when it was judged a continent. Doggerland (sunk by sea-level rise, small) rejected as not a vast land. Zealandia sank by crustal thinning, not a catastrophic Atlantis-style event, so fit is partial.
searched: Wikipedia Zealandia; Crossref record for the 2017 paper.

what: Solatube installed its first prototype tubular daylighting device in Australia: a rooftop light collector sending daylight down a reflective cylinder into the interior.
fit: Collects sunlight with a reflective light guide and conducts it into a building interior for light.

sources.title: Solatube History
sources.quote: First prototype installed The original design features a rooftop light capturing system that redirects daylight through a highly reflective cylinder

note: Earlier candidates: Chappuis reflector systems (1850s, London; Wikipedia gives only a decade) and pavement vault lights (1840s onward), which pass daylight into basements by prisms; judged different mechanisms or undated to the year, so not used. Fiber-optic Himawari sun-tracking systems (Japan, c. 1980) were not verified by a fetched page. Underground or cavern use is not separately dated.
searched: WebSearch (light tube history, Solatube, Himawari), Wikipedia Light tube, solatube.com.

what: First Solatube product sold in Australia.
fit: A commercial light-guide daylighting product used to bring sunlight into buildings.

what: Ascanio Sobrero in Turin synthesized nitroglycerin, a liquid explosive far stronger than black powder.
fit: A liquid chemical explosive much more powerful and shock-sensitive than the gunpowder known at the time.

sources.title: Nitroglycerin
sources.quote: Nitroglycerin was the first practical explosive produced that was stronger than black powder. It was synthesized by the Italian chemist Ascanio Sobrero in 1846

note: Nitrocellulose/guncotton (Schonbein, Bottger, Otto, also 1846) is a contemporaneous solid candidate and equally early; earlier nitrocellulose work (Braconnot 1832, Pelouze 1838) was not shown as a powerful explosive; fulminating mercury (1799) is a sensitive primary explosive but not a bulk 'far more powerful' charge. I dated nitroglycerin (liquid form).
searched: Wikipedia Nitroglycerin, Nitrocellulose, Dynamite.

what: Alfred Nobel patented dynamite (stabilized nitroglycerin) in 1867 and it quickly went into mining and construction use.
fit: A solid, handleable form of the liquid explosive was put to its real blasting purpose as a replacement for black powder.

sources.title: Dynamite
sources.quote: After its introduction, dynamite rapidly gained wide-scale use as a safe alternative to black powder and nitroglycerin.

note: Nobel's blasting oil (liquid nitroglycerin) was used in Sweden from about 1863-64, probably earlier than dynamite, but I did not fetch a source for that date; guncotton was manufactured from 1846 but with limited use.
searched: Wikipedia Dynamite.

what: German Paris Gun fired its first shell on Paris from near Crepy, about 120 km away.

what: General Electric built a demonstration computer from thin-film cryotrons (arrays of 2000 devices operated), following John Bremer's 1957 planar cryotron.

sources.title: Cryotron

what: Southwire energized a high-temperature superconducting power cable at its Carrollton, Georgia plant, feeding three plant facilities with liquid-nitrogen-cooled superconducting cable (18 Feb 2000).

review3: An earlier strict fit than the 2025 'mind captioning' paper: a 2023 decoder wrote out as text what people silently imagined saying.
check_note: Replaces Tang et al. 2023. The definition covers text of thoughts OR mental images/dreams on a screen. Thirion 2006 reconstructs an imagined pattern from fMRI, earlier than the 2023 language decoder; it is crude (a self-chosen pattern from a small set of flickering stimuli), so confidence is low. Rejected as earlier candidates: Farwell and Donchin 1988 P300 speller and Birbaumer 1999 slow-cortical-potential speller (the user picks letters by attention or cursor control; this is selection, not reading out thought content); Vidal 1973 (cursor); Miyawaki 2008 and Nishimoto 2011 (reconstruct images being viewed, not mental images); Horikawa 2013 dream decoding (word categories only); Willett 2021 and Moses 2021 (attempted handwriting or speech); Makin 2020 (spoken sentences). Tang 2023 (PMC11304553, FOUND) is the first decoder of open-ended silent thought into word sequences, the best fit if the checker prefers the text reading of the definition.

note: Streptomycin (Waksman lab, Rutgers; Schatz, Bugie, Waksman 1944) was the first antibiotic active against TB, tested by Feldman and Hinshaw at the Mayo Clinic in guinea pigs in 1944 and in patients from late 1944. Earlier candidates: sanatorium rest (1850s, Brehmer), BCG vaccine (1921, prevention not cure), sulfones/Promin (1940s, weak). Dated the first effective anti-TB drug, with low confidence that it fits "cure" strictly.

sources.quote: keeping the incised surfaces together until they healed

note: John Parker Maynard, a Dedham, Mass., medical student, brushed collodion (nitrocellulose in ether) over the closed edges of a cut and held it with a cotton strap; the account was published in March 1848 and the year 1847 is from later histories, not from the page, so the date is approximate. Earlier candidates: gum and resin plasters, court plaster and sutures (not a sealed film), and the Boston Medical and Surgical Journal says these were the first surgical uses of the mixture. Later: cyanoacrylate glue (Coover 1951-58, used on wounded soldiers in Vietnam in the 1960s, Dermabond approved 1998).

what: Leveaux's spring-driven tram car, built 1874 by Middleton and Co., pulled a passenger car at the Lillie Bridge depot, London; a 5 hp stationary steam engine wound its coiled springs.
fit: Large coiled springs wound by an engine stored the mechanical energy that ran a machine.

sources.title: The Clockwork Tram
sources.quote: It was demonstrated pulling a passenger car at the Lillie Bridge depot of the Metropolitan and District Railway in May 1875.

sources.title: The Clockwork Tram
sources.quote: A small stationary steam engine of about 5 horsepower wound a series of compound coiled springs in barrels

note: Reference source only. Ordinary clockwork and small spring motors are far older but are not large engine-wound storage. Philadelphia spring-car proposals (1883-85) were not built. No spring-powered dynamo or hoist found.
searched: WebSearch on spring tramcars; tramwayinfo.com; archive.org search 'spring motor' street car 1870-1900.

what: Samsung launched the SPH-WP10, a wrist-worn watch phone with built-in speaker and microphone.
fit: A watch-style device on the wrist that makes radio-telephone calls.

sources.title: Smartwatch
sources.quote: In 1999, Samsung launched the world's first watch phone, the SPH-WP10.

note: Dick Tracy-style two-way wrist radios sold in 1947-48 were toys; 1970s-80s wrist radio-telephones appear only as NASA concepts. Mass adoption (cellular smartwatches from about 2017) not sourced, left out.

what: Giovanni Domenico Cassini investigated the zodiacal light and explained it as sunlight scattered by dust around the Sun (some sources credit Fatio de Duillier, 1684).
fit: The explanation attributes the glow to sunlight reflected by orbiting dust, as defined.

sources.title: Zodiacal light
sources.quote: The phenomenon was investigated by the astronomer Giovanni Domenico Cassini in 1683.

sources.title: Zodiacal light
sources.quote: Zodiacal light is produced by sunlight reflecting off dust particles in the Solar System known as cosmic dust.

note: This is an explanation dated by a reference; spectroscopic confirmation (solar spectrum, early 1900s) was not sourced, and Gegenschein backscatter explanation was not separately dated. Joshua Childrey 1661 only reported the light.
